#6369. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

Over the past year, I've redeemed 1.3 million IHG One Rewards points for 62 hotel nights. I got 0.88 cents per point on these redemptions, so while TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of IHG points at 0.6 cents each, it's certainly possible to get more value when redeeming IHG points.

All these redemptions mean I also have to earn a sizable amount of IHG points each year. There are many ways to earn IHG points, so you have options, whether you need to top off your account or substantially boost your balance. In this article, I'll describe how to earn IHG points.

As you might expect, you can earn IHG points when you stay at participating IHG hotels. However, the exact number of points you'll earn on stays depends on a few factors:

You'll only earn IHG points and get access to elite benefits when you book a qualifying rate through a qualifying method. Qualifying methods include IHG Customer Care, IHG websites, the IHG One Rewards app, directly at the hotel and through authorized travel agents. Authorized travel agents exclude online travel agents and are defined in the IHG terms and conditions as "travel booking platforms operating under direct distribution agreements with IHG which specifically provide for nights booked through their platforms to be qualifying stays."

Related: The best IHG hotels in the world

Your earning rate for qualifying stays will vary by IHG hotel brand. Specifically, you'll earn points as follows:

You'll generally earn points on qualifying room rates and additional purchases charged to your room, including food and beverages. However, at some properties, you may not earn points on other purchases charged to your room.

Except at InterContinental Alliance Resorts, you can earn points on up to nine hotel rooms. Your IHG One Rewards account number must be associated with each room reservation, and you must stay at the property.

Members with IHG elite status earn additional points on stays. As you'd expect, the higher your elite status tier, the more points you'll earn on your stay. Here's how many bonus points IHG elite members will earn:

Here's an example of how these bonus points can add up. If you're a Diamond Elite member staying at a Kimpton hotel for three nights at $200 per night, you'll earn the following:

As a result, you'd take home 12,000 IHG points from your three-night stay — and potentially more if you made any qualifying charges to your room or paid for your stay with a rewards card. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, 12,000 IHG One Rewards points are worth $72.

You can often buy up to 5,000 elite qualifying points per night when booking a qualifying paid stay. Look for the option on the "Add Extras" page while booking.

There's no cap on the number of points you can buy each calendar year via these packages. As such, doing so can be a good option if you have already reached the maximum number of points you can outright purchase in a calendar year.

Starting at just 20 nights a year, IHG members earn a choice of Milestone Rewards for every 10 nights (up to 100 nights per year). IHG offers its members various rewards at each milestone, and some may be more valuable than points.

But if you're primarily interested in earning IHG points, you can choose points at each milestone. Specifically, you can earn points through Milestone Rewards each calendar year as follows:

I rarely choose points as Milestone Rewards, as I usually find food-and-beverage rewards, confirmable suite upgrade awards or an annual lounge membership provides more value.

IHG One Rewards frequently offers promotions that let you earn additional points on your hotel stays over the standard earning rates. However, you usually need to register for IHG bonus points promotions before completing your stay.

For IHG promotions that offer multipliers (such as double points), the multiplier typically applies only to the stay's base earnings. So, if you are an IHG elite member, your elite bonus usually won't be multiplied.

Related: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards

One of the easiest ways to earn IHG points is by spending on a cobranded IHG credit card. Here's how the four currently available IHG credit cards earn points, including their updated earning categories beginning Jan. 1, 2027 (see the paragraph below the table for some additional earning rates that end Dec. 31):

Through Dec. 31, IHG Premier and Business cardholders will also earn 5 points per dollar spent on all other travel, while no-annual-fee IHG cardholders will also earn 3 points per dollar spent on utilities, internet, cable, phone services and select streaming services.

Cardholders of the Premier, Premier Select and Business cards get automatic access to the valuable IHG fourth-night-free reward perk. But cardholders of the no-annual-fee IHG card will need to spend $5,000 or more with their card within a calendar year to unlock access to the fourth-night-free reward perk through the end of the next calendar year starting in 2027. I've used the fourth-night-free reward perk 13 times during the last year, so it provides a ton of value to me.

Related: The best IHG hotel stays you can book with 200,000 points

You can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Bilt Points to the IHG One Rewards program. Points transfer at a 1:1 ratio from both programs.

However, I don't recommend transferring points from either program to IHG. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd need to redeem IHG points for at least 2.05 cents each to justify transferring Chase points or 2.2 cents each to justify transferring Bilt points.

As such, you'll generally only want to transfer points to IHG if you need to top off your account for a specific award. Otherwise, saving transferable points for higher-value redemptions is generally better.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

The IHG One Rewards Dine & Earn program allows you to earn points when you dine at participating restaurants and bars. To use the program, you must sign up for an account online and link at least one credit or debit card to your account. Then, you'll automatically earn IHG points when you use a linked card to pay at participating restaurants and bars.

The points you'll earn vary depending on how frequently you use the program and whether you opt in for email notifications. You can earn between 1 and 8 IHG points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. These points are in addition to the rewards earned on your credit card, so consider linking and using one of the best cards for dining purchases.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

You can also earn IHG points through the IHG Business Rewards program. This program allows you to earn points when you plan a meeting or event — including a wedding — at select IHG properties.

Once you register for IHG Business Rewards, you can earn 3 points per dollar when you book rooms, meetings and events for others. Qualifying spending includes:

Some properties don't participate in IHG Business Rewards. And you usually can't earn more than 60,000 points on a meeting or event. Plus, qualifying spending usually excludes taxes, gratuities, service fees and the organizer's room.

Another option for earning IHG points is to purchase them. Buying IHG points can be a good deal, especially when the program offers a 100% bonus and you have a high-value redemption in mind.

The standard price to buy IHG points is 1 cent per point if you purchase at least 26,000 points. However, IHG One Rewards offers promotions several times a year during which you can purchase points with up to a 100% bonus. If you buy during a 100% bonus, you can earn IHG points for as little as 0.5 cents each.

TPG values IHG points at 0.6 cents each. Since it's easy for me to get more than 0.5 cents of value per IHG point, I usually consider purchasing IHG points whenever there's a 100% bonus sale. However, you usually can't purchase more than 200,000 IHG points per calendar year.

IHG members can transfer points to another member by paying a $5 fee per 1,000 points transferred. Each member can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year and receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year.

IHG members who hold Diamond Elite status — or belong to the IHG Business Rewards program and have "consumed a Business Rewards event in the current or previous calendar year" — can transfer points to other members without paying transfer fees.

So, if you have a colleague or family member who has Diamond Elite status (or is an active member of the IHG Business Rewards program) and wants to transfer IHG points to you, this could be a way to earn IHG points.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

Throughout this guide, we've discussed how to earn IHG points that you can redeem for hotel stays. However, travelers looking to earn IHG elite status should also consider which points qualify for elite status.

Generally, the following activities earn IHG points that are redeemable and elite qualifying:

On the other hand, the following activities usually earn points that are redeemable but not elite qualifying (unless otherwise indicated):

Related: How to maximize award redemptions with the IHG One Rewards program

There are plenty of ways to earn IHG One Rewards points, from staying at IHG hotels and using cobranded credit cards to dining out and booking rental cars. You can also buy points when IHG offers a good promotion.

I frequently get significantly more than TPG's valuation of 0.6 cents per IHG point when redeeming for hotel stays, so I find it worthwhile to keep a decent balance. However, I'd generally avoid transferring valuable Chase Ultimate Rewards points or Bilt points to IHG unless you need to top off your account for a specific redemption.

#6367. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. But perhaps the most lovable feature is the private backyard, which has a pool, firepit, and full dining table, all surrounded by lush greenery and sleek appliances.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Observatory Park, The Robert and Judi Newman Center for the Performing Arts, University Hills Farmers Market, University of Denver

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: California king bed, flat-screen TV, immersive sound system, disco ball, LED lighting, faux-fire Malm fireplace, skyline views

Get groovy at this nostalgic studio apartment, which features an authentic disco ball and skyline views (including a peek at Coors Field, where the Colorado Rockies play) in the heart of Denver's Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood. Lucky for its guests, this spot is within walking distance of downtown Denver’s hottest entertainment, shopping, and dining outposts for a day or night out on the town. Plus, it’s equipped with all the amenities of your dreams, including a spacious California king bed, a 13-foot vintage couch, and a fully equipped kitchen for whipping up meals.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Coors Field, Commons Park, Little Man Ice Cream shop, Ball Arena, 16th Street Mall, Larimer Square, McGregor Square, Denver Union Station

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, fully equipped kitchen, private backyard, in-unit washer and dryer, kid-friendly amenities

You and your crew are in for a treat when staying at this charming, historic Boulder home. With original woodwork, colorful wallpaper, a fenced backyard, and three spacious bedrooms, guests here will enjoy a stylish stay.

Its location is the true star of the show: Right off Pearl Street, Boulder's happening hub of art, food, and entertainment venues, you'll be within walking distance from it all. Previous guests have raved about not having to rent a car when booking this base; even the airport bus takes you within three blocks of the address.

City: BoulderThings to do nearby: The Museum of Boulder, Pearl Street Mall, Boulder Theater, Pearl Street

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Rocky Mountain views, hot tub, outdoor kitchen with gas grill, firepit, Dobsonian telescope

Tucked on five private acres, this is a true mountain retreat in Bailey—a Colorado town less than an hour outside Denver, known for its quirky roadside attractions, outdoor recreation, and historic mountain charm. Dubbed “Skytrail Lodge,” this cabin fits right into the neighborhood.

The main living area is bright and welcoming, with floor-to-ceiling windows that bring the outside in. A big, comfy sofa anchors the living room, complemented by green and black accents that create an upscale, modern feel. Outside, lounge about on the deck and take in the incredible view of the Rocky Mountains. What better place to sip on your morning cup of joe, read a book, or indulge in an evening glass of wine?

City: BaileyThings to do nearby: Mount Bailey, Pine Valley Ranch Park, Brookside-McCurdy Trailhead, Crooked Top Mountain, Shawnee

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to ski resort, private hot tub, chef's kitchen, spacious design, smart TVs

Tucked in the storybook town of Cascade Village, you'll find a stay that exudes real mountain charm, with creature comforts to write home about. This Vail house is just a five-minute walk to Vail Ski Resort, with a free shuttle to Lionshead and Vail Village nearby. Meaning no matter the season—whether skiing or hiking—guests will have a convenient stay accompanied by the amenities that make an Airbnb great: a private, six-person hot tub; a fully equipped kitchen; en suite soaking tubs; private balcony access; and a laundry area.

Folks who stay here can cook up dinner on the grill or in the spacious kitchen, enjoy their meals in the eight-person dining area, play some groovy tunes on the Sonos speaker, and sip on a cup of coffee while looking out over the city and mountains. If you needed a sign to book a fun group adventure, consider this it.

City: VailThings to do nearby: Eagle Bahn Gondola, Lionshead Village, Vail Village, Ford Park, Betty Ford Alpine Gardens

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, wood-burning fireplace, shared hot tubs and heated pool, private patio

If you're looking for a stay in a mountain city that's as convenient as it is cozy, this Breckenridge condo is your solution. The renovated two-bedroom town house is designed for folks interested in exploring the downtown pubs, restaurants, and art-filled spaces—as well as the mountain trails, ski resorts, and beautiful natural surroundings.

Back at the rental, use the space to “ski, stroll, soak, and repeat,” as stated in the listing. Unwind around the crackling wood-burning fireplace, enjoy a home-cooked meal around the big dining table, stay in for a round of board games, or indulge in one of the condo's shared amenities: the heated pool, sauna, or one of the four hot tubs.

City: BreckenridgeThings to do nearby: Illinois Creek Trailhead, Carter Park and Pavilion, Breckenridge Brewery & Pub, South Main Street, QuickSilver SuperChair

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, wraparound deck, wood-burning fireplace, mountain views

Say hello to your next base for that upcoming group trip. This three-story timber lodge is all about space, convenience, and mountain fun. With a light-filled, open-concept kitchen and living room, you'll have some room to breathe. The floor-to-ceiling windows with sprawling mountain views and a wraparound deck make it even better. The home sits only 12 miles from Breckenridge, so it's drivable to the city's best hubs—from nature to dining—while also being tucked away enough to sprawl out and frolic.

Aside from the four queen bedrooms, there's a game room complete with a foosball table, vintage arcade games, table tennis, and more, making it a truly kid-friendly base.

City: AlmaThings to do nearby: Peaceful Valley Lodge, Wheeler Lake Winter Trailhead, Downtown Breckenridge, Montgomery Reservoir

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

With its ski-in/ski-out location and proximity to one of the lifts on Aspen Mountain, this is a stellar booking for snow chasers. But it's also a fantastic base for those heading to Aspen in the warmer months, thanks to its swanky year-round amenities, like a sprawling pool and hot tub with lounge chairs for relaxing or soaking up the sun.

City: AspenThings to do nearby: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort (one block to Lift 1A), Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bedsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, sauna, mountain views, wood-burning stove, design-forward interiors

This swanky cabin is ideal for those in need of a restorative nature trip. The cool cabin aesthetic extends throughout the open-concept kitchen, big windows, hot tub, and sauna—and the view of the sprawling mountain range is well appreciated.

The biggest peak you can see from the living room is the region's iconic La Plata, which is the fifth-highest in the Rockies. Mount Elbert, Colorado's highest peak, is at the back of the home, with one of its trailheads a few minutes down the road. Another big plus? The home sits just over a two-hour drive from Denver—making it a sweet weekend trip for Mile High City locals and a good road trip stop for those heading onward.

City: Twin LakesThings to do nearby: Rinker Peak, Independence Pass, Mount Elbert, Twin Lakes Village, Colorado Trail, Continental Divide Trail, Leadville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, hot tub, tasteful interior design, barbecue grill with outdoor seating

The lush Glenwood Springs is an underrated gem compared to its more frequented neighbors, Grand Junction and Moab. At this one-of-a-kind cabin, though, you'll likely question why it's taken you so long to plan a trip here in the first place.

Awe-inspiring canyon views await in every room through expansive windows, adding to the spot's light and airy feel. Each bedroom features a Tempur-Pedic bed and private deck access for true comfort and solitude. Indulge in the outdoor perks, too—there's a six-person hot tub, a firepit on the patio, and a four-person barrel sauna ready for post-adventure restoration. You'll also have prime access to the village's downtown square and its iconic hot springs.

City: Glenwood SpringsThings to do nearby: Colorado River, No Name Trailhead, Lookout Mountain, South Canyon Hot Springs, Horse Mountain, Hanging Lake Trailhead

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Mountain and forest views, private patio, bathtub, indoor fireplace, Wi-Fi

As one of Airbnb's most wishlisted properties, find this spruced-up, octagon-shaped tree house tucked away in the small mountain community of Cascade. It’s a scenic 15-minute drive from Colorado Springs, but you’ll find serenity easily among the tree house's natural surroundings. With floor-to-ceiling windows that look out to a little forest paradise, a wood-burning stove, a coffee and waffle maker, puzzles, games, and a smart TV, you'll never want to leave.

If you do plan to go out, you’re just five minutes away from Pikes Peak Highway, dotted with loads of gorgeous hiking trails, but you don’t have to leave your property to catch a glimpse of hummingbirds and other wildlife.

City: Cascade-Chipita ParkThings to do nearby: Ski and/or trails, scenic drives, Woodland Park, restaurants, reservoirs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Pikes Peak views, convenient location, fully equipped kitchen, opt-in grocery delivery

This lofty town house—positioned (basically) right next to Garden of the Gods public park—is all about the views. The kitchen, living, and dining room all face the iconic Pikes Peak through a glass garage door. When open, it transforms the space into a picture-perfect indoor-outdoor area, complete with an overhanging balcony for taking it all in.

Two of the three spacious bedrooms sit on the home's ground level with shared bathroom space. There's also a separate “kids room,” complete with two twin beds—plus a trundle and space to hang out with a television (and a game system). You might not want to spend too much time at home, though: The home sits just a few blocks from Manitou Springs and Old Colorado City for sightseeing, restaurant trips, outdoor adventures, and more.

City: Colorado SpringsThings to do nearby: Manitou, Red Rocks, Garden of the Gods, Old Colorado City, Academy Riding Stables, The Incline, The Cog Railway

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Quirky design, infrared sauna, firepit, mountain and valley views

Just a one-hour drive from Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, this otherworldly home deserves a spot on your Colorado bucket list. It sits at the base of the Sangre de Cristo range, with mountain views by day and dark skies for stargazing at night. As one of the quirkiest picks on this list, this hobbit home has more creature comforts than appear at first glance. There's a kitchenette for meals at home, a dining table that seats four, and an in-unit washer and dryer. You'll also find an infrared sauna to relax in, as well as a firepit to cozy up around. Do note, the home is most ideal for duos or small families, with its one queen bedroom and a double bed in the loft.

City: CrestoneThings to do nearby: Great Sand Dunes National Park, Blueberry Peak, Duncan, Eureka Mountain, Sangre de Cristo Mountain Range

#6366. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6365. Best Things to Do in Hamilton, Ontario

A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something new therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

Hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

The house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a big museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how important the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

The Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:

Webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

Important Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

Spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

The Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

Hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

Hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

The Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a big part of the city’s story.

ThGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

The Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

Hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

This is the kind of event that shows how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Plan your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

The Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most important artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

Hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre company and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

You can find fresh produce, cheese, meat, baked goods, prepared foods, coffee, and international food stalls, plus it is a great lunch stop, especially if you are visiting the Art Gallery of Hamilton or exploring downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t just shop. Plan to eat here. It is one of the easiest ways to sample Hamilton’s food scene in one place.

Born & Raised is one of the best restaurants to pair with a visit to James Street North, as it is located right in the Art Crawl district, it is surrounded by galleries, shops, cafes, and the creative energy that makes this part of Hamilton so fun.

The restaurant was created by chef Vittorio Colacitti and focuses on bold flavours, Italian-inspired dishes, pizza, and a lively neighbourhood atmosphere. It is a great choice for dinner after Art Crawl or a night out downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are visiting during James Street Art Crawl, make a reservation if possible because the street gets busy, and this is exactly the kind of place you’ll want to settle into after walking the galleries.

King William Street has become one of Hamilton’s best dining areas, with restaurants, patios, and cocktail spots packed into a walkable downtown strip especially if you want a more polished dinner, this is a good area to explore.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: King William is a great choice if you want to turn a Hamilton day trip into an evening out.

Hamilton is a great family day trip because many attractions are easy to combine. therefore good family-friendly stops include:

The key with kids is not to overpack the day. Pick one museum, one outdoor stop, and one easy food stop.

Hamilton can be a budget-friendly day trip if you plan it well.

Always check parking and reservation requirements before visiting waterfalls or conservation areas.

Yes, Hamilton is worth visiting because it combines waterfalls, hiking trails, museums, waterfront parks, restaurants, art galleries, and local culture in one easy day trip or weekend getaway. It has the outdoor appeal of the Niagara Escarpment, the history of an old industrial city, and the food and arts scene of a place that has reinvented itself without losing its character.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it is close enough for a full-day visit but different enough to feel like a real change of scenery. You can tour Dundurn Castle, hike to waterfalls, walk the waterfront, visit the Art Gallery of Hamilton, and end the day with dinner on James Street North.

Hamilton is best known for its industrial history, waterfalls, hiking trails, the Niagara Escarpment, arts scene, food scene, and waterfront. It is still called “Steeltown,” but today it is just as well known for outdoor adventure, creative neighbourhoods, and one of Ontario’s most underrated city breaks.

Spring, summer, and fall are the best times to visit Hamilton for waterfalls, hiking, gardens, patios, festivals, and James Street Art Crawl. Fall is especially beautiful in the Dundas Valley, while winter is better for museums, restaurants, theatre, the Royal Botanical Gardens, and indoor attractions.

A car is useful in Hamilton, especially if you want to visit waterfalls, conservation areas, Dundas, Stoney Creek, the Royal Botanical Gardens, or attractions outside downtown. Once you are downtown, areas like James Street North, King William Street, the farmers’ market, and the Art Gallery of Hamilton are much easier to explore on foot.

#6364. The 50 Best Restaurants For 2026 Have Been Announced—With a Remote European Spot in First Place

The 50 Best Restaurants for 2026 have just been announced as part of a prestigious awards ceremony in Lima on Wednesday, November 5, 2026. As with every year, we wait for the release—an indicator of which restaurants will be topping travelers' lists in the year ahead, and the trends that will shape the experiences they offer. Below, we cover which restaurant snagged the top spot, which restaurant led on every continent, and the industry stars celebrated with individual awards like Best Pastry Chef, Best Sommelier, and more.

Read on for the full list, and notable takeaways from the winners. (For more on the trends revealed at the Lima event, read our reporter's conversation with winning chefs here.)

The Best Restaurant in the World for 2026 is hidden away in sleepy Basque village, Axpe.

Climbing up from its number two spot in last year's list, this year’s winner is Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, in Spain's Basque Country.

Basque wood-fired cooking is at the heart of this rustic fine-dining restaurant. Chef-owner Víctor Arguinzoniz (also known as Bittor Arginzoniz) is considered a pioneer of grilling and live-fire cooking. At Asador Etxebarri, every course of Bittor Arginzoniz's €300 euro (about $337 USD) tasting menu touches the wood and charcoal grills—from Palamós red prawns to smoked milk ice cream.

Hidden away in the sleepy mountain village of Axpe, about 45 minutes by car from Bilbao, foodies have been making the pilgrimage to try Arguinzoniz's signature grilled dishes since the restaurant opened in 1990. It's been an 18-year journey to the top, as Asador Etxebarri has been a mainstay on The World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2008, starting at number 44.

Once a restaurant gets the coveted number-one trophy, it is ineligible for nomination in forthcoming years—with the intention of allowing other restaurants a chance to earn top billing. Top-placing restaurants are then inducted into a new list, called the Best of the Best. This list includes such legendary eateries as Chef Thomas Keller's The French Laundry in Yountville, California, and Disfrutar in Barcelona, Spain. Last year’s winner, Maido in Lima, Peru, is the most recent inductee to this prestigious list.

It’s tempting to imagine the enviable job held by a panel of judges that sample every restaurant in the world. But that’s not quite how the 50 Best works. Rather, the 50 is an international media company that taps the expertise of over a thousand hospitality experts from around the world to weigh in on the industry that they know best. Chefs, restaurateurs, food journalists, and well-traveled gourmets all anonymously nominate restaurants that they have dined at within the last 18 months. (Members can’t vote for a restaurant they have a financial interest in.) Professional services consultancy Deloitte has access to the voting data to ensure the validity and fairness of the process.

Because of the voting-style nature of the awards, a restaurant might fall off the list one year only to return later. This year, previous entries to the list such as The Ledbury—a fine-dining beauty in London, United Kingdom where chef Brett Graham marries British produce, Japanese flavours, and French culinary techniques—returns to the list in the number 83 spot. Similarly, Luxe Mosu in Seoul, South Korea—home to chef Sung Anh's elevated interpretations of traditional Korean fare—returns to the list at number 78.

“Every year The 50 Best Restaurants list gives us a snapshot of where more than 1,100 individuals who live and breathe this industry have had their most memorable restaurant experiences over the previous 18 months," explains Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50. “And I think that’s what makes it so special. Each Academy member votes independently, so nobody at The 50 or any of our partners has a say in who makes the list, and restaurants can’t nominate themselves. This means every restaurant on the list has genuinely earned it.”

Gaggan in Bangkok climbed up to Number 2 after placing at Number 6 the year prior.

As always, the highest-ranking restaurants on each continent have been given a special mention during tonight's awards—and there are a few repeats from last year. Gaggan in Bangkok (this year's number 2) won the best restaurant in Asia again. Mexico City's Quintonil (4) was the best restaurant in Latin America again, while New York City's Atomix (11) was the best restaurant in North America. Dubai's Trèsind Studio (28) was named the best restaurant in the Middle East for another year. The best restaurant in Africa was Cape Town's La Colombe (35). Sydney's Saint Peter (50) was the best restaurant in Oceania, while top spot Asador Etxebarri took the best restaurant in Europe award.

Every year, the panel awards special prizes to chefs, front-of-house staff, and activists who are leading the charge in hospitality. In 2026, the Best Female Chef Award went to Jessica Rosval, head chef of Al Gatto Verde. Bangkok’s Dej Kewkacha won Best Pastry Chef Award, and Lesley Liu of Odette in Singapore won the Best Sommelier Award while the Estrella Damm Chefs' Choice Award went to Junghyun ‘JP’ Park from Atomix in New York City. Doris Lam won The 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship. Spanish chef Ferran Adrià of El Bulli won the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Restaurants given a special mention during the 2026 ceremony included Tuju in São Paulo, which earned the Highest New Entry Award. Copenhagen's Kadeau won the Highest Climber Award after soaring 33 places this year, and Naar in Kasauli, India, won the Sustainable Restaurant Award.

This year, only one US restaurant made the top 50: Atomix, in New York. It came in 11th place, rising one place from 2025, when it ranked 12.
