I get asked some version of the same question all the time: what’s the best travel credit card to actually keep in your wallet?

For me, the answer has changed over time. As my travel habits have evolved, so has the mix of cards I rely on. Some help me earn points quickly, others offset travel costs with built-in credits, and a few simply make traveling more comfortable.

While getting outsize value from a travel credit card often means paying an annual fee, I've found that the right perks can more than justify the cost. And one of the cards I'm looking to add to my wallet next doesn't charge an annual fee at all.

These are the travel credit cards I keep coming back to — and in some cases, the ones I'm planning to add next — based on their earning potential, flexibility and benefits I actually find useful.

I chose these cards based on the value they can provide travelers. In particular, I considered:

I've also included cards for different types of travelers, from beginners and those seeking premium perks to airline and hotel loyalists and travelers who don't want to pay an annual fee.

Purchases that qualify for the $300 annual travel credit will not earn points.

*The top brands are Airbnb, Vrbo, Plum Guide, HomeAway, Homestay.com and Vacasa

*Welcome offer value is an estimated value based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by the issuer.

The newest premium travel card in my wallet is the , and after just a few months, it's already become one of my favorites.

While the $795 annual fee is steep, I've been getting plenty of use out of the card's travel perks. One of my favorite benefits so far has been the up to $500 in annual credits for The Edit, Chase’s curated hotel booking platform (issued as two credits of up to $250 per calendar year for stays of two nights or more).

I recently used one of those credits for a luxury stay at At Six in Stockholm, where I also enjoyed some of the other perks when you book with The Edit, such as complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit. The hotel's impressive breakfast spread was a particular highlight, and I was able to use the property credit to cover a couple of dine-in meals.

Lounge access has also been a major benefit. I frequently fly through Dulles International Airport (IAD) when visiting family on the East Coast, and the Etihad Lounge, which is part of the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, has become one of my go-to spots to relax before a flight.

I've also booked other hotel stays through Chase Travel, where the card earns 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. Between the hotel benefits, lounge access and $300 annual travel credit, I've found plenty of ways to put the Reserve to work in a short period of time.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 valuable points

The was the first travel card in my wallet — and that goes for a lot of us here at TPG. It’s also the card I recommend most often to beginners or casual travelers who want flexible points without a sky-high annual fee.

With beginner-friendly perks like a $100 annual hotel credit and strong travel protections, it delivers real value without overwhelming complexity.

The card also makes it easy to get quick, upfront value. After earning the welcome offer and maximizing bonus categories — like 3 points per dollar spent on dining and 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchased outside the Chase Travel portal — I was able to build a sizable stash of points within a few months.

I ultimately redeemed those points for a trip through four European countries, which felt like a pretty great return for my first year with the card.

I'm also particularly excited about the card's newer earning category for vacation rentals. As someone who's stayed in more than 60 Airbnbs, I love that I can now earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation home rentals, including Airbnb bookings.

It’s the travel card I recommend over and over again to friends and family because of its ease of use, strong earning potential and outsize value relative to its modest $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred.

Related: 6 ways to maximize the Chase Sapphire Preferred as a beginner

Best for: Straightforward premium rewards

Another top contender in the premium space — and one that’s firmly earned a place in my wallet — is the Capital One Venture X Rewards Card. For me, its biggest selling point is how easy it is to get value from the card without having to overthink my spending.

Part of the reason I added the card was to diversify my points and miles beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards. Up until recently, I’d been almost exclusively earning Chase points, but as I’ve gotten deeper into the points and miles world, I’ve realized how valuable it is to have access to multiple transferable currencies and transfer partners.

At the same time, the Venture X fits naturally into my everyday spending habits. Cardholders earn a flat 2 miles per dollar on nearly every purchase, which removes the need to track bonus categories or optimize every swipe. It’s become my go-to catch-all card and the one I reach for whenever a purchase doesn’t neatly fit into a bonus category on another card.

I've also gotten great use out of its travel benefits. I recently used the card's $300 annual Capital One Travel credit toward a three-night stay at the DoubleTree by Hilton London Marble Arch, bringing the cost down from $1,096 to $796. I also appreciate being able to relax in Capital One Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges when I travel.

For me, the Venture X works because it combines straightforward everyday earning with travel benefits I actually use, making its $395 annual fee easier to justify.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Related: 5 reasons why I’m applying for the Capital One Venture X

For travelers who regularly fly a single airline — especially those based near one of that carrier’s hubs — a cobranded airline card can make a lot of sense.

That’s been true for me with United, but I think the same general strategy applies to frequent Delta and American Airlines flyers as well. If you consistently fly one carrier, the right airline card can make your travel experience cheaper, smoother and more comfortable through perks like travel credits, free checked bags and priority boarding.

Despite its $350 annual fee, the offers several easy-to-use benefits that help offset the cost. The $200 annual United travel credit, for instance, has helped offset flights home to visit family. And the two free checked bags for me and a travel companion have already saved me a significant amount in baggage fees.

The card also offers award flight discounts, anniversary bonus miles, priority boarding and improved award availability, which make the card feel like a keeper for the long term.

That said, I do wish it included lounge access — especially at this price point.

Still, the Quest has made flying United more affordable and convenient for me, which is exactly what I want from an airline credit card.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

Not every worthwhile travel rewards card needs to charge an annual fee. The is one I'm interested in adding to my wallet because it could fill an important gap in my Chase strategy without adding another annual fee.

On its own, the Freedom Unlimited earns cash-back rewards. But when you pair it with an eligible Ultimate Rewards-earning card like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you can combine your rewards and potentially get more value by redeeming them for travel or transferring them to Chase's airline and hotel partners.

That's particularly appealing to me because I'm working toward building the Chase Trifecta, a strategy that combines multiple Chase cards to maximize earnings across different types of purchases.

With no annual fee, the Freedom Unlimited could give me another way to earn rewards on everyday spending while letting my Sapphire cards handle travel purchases and unlock more valuable redemption options.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Related: The best beginner Chase card combo for travel rewards

Best for: Hilton perks without the premium price tag

The is the newest addition to my wallet — and my first hotel credit card.

For years, I've prioritized flexible rewards over hotel-specific points because I didn't want to commit to a single hotel program. But as I've started traveling more and spending more nights in hotels, I realized I was leaving some valuable perks on the table.

After comparing several hotel cards, I ultimately chose the Hilton Surpass because it struck the right balance between cost and benefits. One of the biggest draws for me is automatic Hilton Honors Gold status, which gives me meaningful hotel perks without requiring me to earn status through stays.

I'm also a fan of the card's up to $200 in Hilton statement credits each calendar year, issued as up to $50 each quarter. And Hilton's large footprint means I'm much more likely to find a property where I can actually put those benefits to use when I travel.

For me, the Surpass is a relatively approachable way to test-drive hotel loyalty while getting useful benefits from the start. As I spend more nights with Hilton, I'll be able to see whether a hotel card deserves a permanent place in my travel strategy.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass.

Related: How I chose my first hotel credit card — and the 4 cards I considered

Choosing the right travel credit card ultimately comes down to how you travel, where you spend your money and which perks you'll actually use.

For beginners, the Chase Sapphire Preferred remains one of the strongest entry points thanks to its balance of value, flexibility and simplicity. Frequent travelers looking for a more premium experience — especially when it comes to lounge access and travel perks — may get more value from the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Meanwhile, the Capital One Venture X is a great fit for travelers who want premium benefits without overcomplicating their rewards strategy, and the United Quest offers a strong value proposition for frequent United flyers who prioritize convenience and United-specific perks.

For travelers who don't want to add another annual fee, the Chase Freedom Unlimited can be a useful complement to a Sapphire card, particularly if you're building a Chase trifecta. And for travelers who want hotel-specific perks, the Hilton Surpass offers a relatively accessible entry point to hotel loyalty with automatic Hilton Gold status and useful Hilton credits.

You certainly don't need all six cards on this list to get good value from travel rewards. But whether you're looking for your first travel card or considering adding another to your wallet, I'd start by thinking about which benefits you'd use most often — and whether they're worth the annual fee.

#6341. Singapore Airlines Unveils New Business Class Suites With Doors, Companion Beds, And More Room To Sleep

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its next-generation long-haul business class seat, adding sliding doors, redesigned sleeping space, and center seats that can form companion beds. The most interesting change may be the footwell: the airline has redesigned how the table stows to give passengers more room to move their feet while sleeping.

I already wrote about the new first class suites here.

The new business class product was designed by Designworks, a BMW Group company, and manufactured by the German firm RECARO Aircraft Seating. It will be installed on Boeing 777-9 aircraft and retrofitted Airbus A350-900 long-haul and A350-900ULR aircraft. Every seat will have direct aisle access in a 1-2-1 configuration.

The product will not be identical across aircraft. The Boeing version will have a wider seat, while the Airbus version will feature a larger entertainment screen.

The fully flat bed measures 79 inches long and up to 24 inches wide. Selected center seats can be configured as companion beds when the divider is lowered, which appears to be every other row.

The published bed width is “up to” 24 inches, which I read as saying there will not be a uniform 24-inch-wide sleeping surface from shoulder to foot.

The leather-upholstered seat offers adjustable upper and lower lumbar support and a leg rest easily accessible control buttons should make it easier to adjust the seat without hunting through a touchscreen menu.

Singapore Airlines is also adding a padded bedsheet incorporating memory foam, which it says can provide additional cushioning when sleeping or be used for lumbar support while seated.

Integrated myKrisWorld controls will save a passenger’s preferred seat position for future journeys. Multiple storage compartments, wireless charging, and universal A/C power will be included.

On the A350, the seat is 22 inches wide, with a 22-inch 4K OLED screen. On the 777-9, the seat measures 24 inches across, but the screen is a smaller 20-inch 4K display.

Both offer Bluetooth headphone pairing and supplied noise-canceling headphones. The entertainment handset also displays flight information, destination weather, Wi-Fi status, and lavatory availability.

The new cabins are scheduled to enter service progressively from the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines has also announced a progressive Starlink rollout on its A350 long-haul and ULR aircraft from early 2027. That is a separate installation program, so new connectivity will likely occur before the aircraft has new seats.

#6340. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6339. Delta Air Lines Boosts Summer 2027 Schedule With New Routes & Expanded Weekend Frequencies

Delta Air Lines has announced another expansion of its summer 2027 network, featuring 11 seasonal routes, additional weekend frequencies on five domestic services, and increased flying to 10 Latin American and Caribbean destinations. The changes announced today target leisure travelers heading to mountain resorts, national parks, and beach destinations.

The strategy builds on Delta's summer 2026 expansion, which introduced Saturday-only flights from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) alongside returning seasonal services elsewhere. Analysis of newly available Department Of Transportation (DOT) data reveals that numerous routes achieved load factors exceeding 90%, explaining why Delta is maintaining its focus on weekend leisure demand while selectively increasing capacity.

Delta's latest announcement features 11 routes originating from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW), Austin and Los Angeles. All appeared in the airline's original summer 2026 plans, with destinations including Bozeman, Kalispell, Jackson Hole and Pensacola.

Most services begin in late May or June, although flights to Bangor will continue into October, extending beyond the traditional summer vacation period. Importantly, Detroit–Destin represents a reinstatement, having been canceled before summer 2026 operations began.

Airbus A319, Boeing 717, Bombardier CRJ700

While a once-weekly service might seem thin, it taps into leisure travelers who want to get away for a week and seek new destinations. This travel segment has surged post-pandemic, and Delta is betting that the trend will continue in 2027.

Amy Martin, Delta's Vice President of Network Planning, spoke about the latest expansion.

“We’re continuing to tailor Delta’s schedule around where our customers want to travel. By adding weekend flights to some of the most sought-after leisure destinations, we’re giving customers more flexibility and more ways to make the most of their summer.”

The airline is also including eight previously loaded Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) routes, serving destinations such as Charleston, Savannah and Halifax, alongside two Florida connections from LaGuardia Airport (LGA). These additions complement Delta's wider Boston expansion, which includes new European connections for 2027.

The return of these routes suggests that Delta found success with them this past summer, and analysis of the DOT's T-100 data indicates this was definitely the case. Detroit–Pensacola achieved the highest June-July 2026 average load factor at 95.5%, followed by Atlanta-Bangor at 92.2% and Atlanta-Rapid City at 91.5%. Detroit-Bangor and Detroit-Bozeman also performed strongly, averaging approximately 89%, suggesting particularly robust demand from established Delta hubs.

However, newer routes didn't perform at those levels, with Austin-Bozeman, Austin-Kalispell, and Los Angeles-Jackson Hole all operating below 80% full. Nevertheless, Delta has already extended Austin-Bozeman into winter, when it will operate daily during peak ski season. Such decisions illustrate why summer occupancy alone cannot determine profitability or a route's longer-term potential.

Delta is also increasing capacity on five established domestic routes, adding a weekend frequency to each. The changes include Orlando and Fort Myers service from Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG), beginning in April, while Minneapolis–Kalispell receives more flying from June. These enhancements suggest Delta is selectively investing in established markets alongside its returning leisure experiments.

The airline will be adding 13 new Saturday-only routes from six of its hubs as part of its Summer 2026 schedule.

International leisure expansion forms another major component of Delta's plans. 10 routes across Latin America and the Caribbean will receive additional Saturday frequencies, extended operating seasons, or both. Atlanta accounts for half, with the airline highlighting a new Saturday flight to St. Lucia that will improve connections through its largest hub.

Delta's latest expansion consequently emphasizes refining existing networks rather than introducing large numbers of entirely new destinations. Strong 2026 load factors on several routes help explain the strategy, though the return of slightly weaker performers suggests other considerations, including seasonal yields and aircraft utilization. With fuel costs encouraging greater capacity discipline, targeted weekend flying lets Delta pursue leisure growth without substantial year-round commitments.

#6338. This Swanky Service Lets Commercial Fliers Skip the Airport Entirely—And It's Now Available in Dallas and Miami

As my plane touched down in Dallas, I could already make out my chauffeur waiting on the apron, the jet-black SUV glimmering in the Texas sun. It wasn’t long before my luggage was whisked away and we were driving across the airfield, past rows of planes waiting at their gates—so close that I could read their tail numbers. Our destination? A new private terminal operated by the company PS, which offers a curious promise to commercial fliers: Travel with us, and you will never step foot in the airport.

The shared “Salon” area at the PS Dallas Terminal, included in the entry-level pricing. Access to private suites cost an additional fee based on membership status.

Ten minutes later, my driver dropped me off at PS’s sleek new 12,200-square-foot private terminal at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), where I was greeted by caviar and Champagne and escorted to my own private suite. Between the goodie-filled drawers, marble sinks, and the rainfall shower, I could have spent my whole time in the bathroom, where I had my pick of Le Labo products, plush towels, and comfy robes. It wasn’t like any airport lounge I had ever been to, rivaling even first class. And yet, it's still a fraction of the cost of flying private.

Champagne and caviar at the PS private suite.

PS first launched at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in 2017, then called “The Private Suite.” As the name implies, all PS terminals have their own private, line-free TSA security screenings and dedicated Customs and Immigration checkpoints separate from the crowds. While this has earned the brand a reputation of being a “celebrity terminal," PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter says public figures actually make up "a very, very small portion" of the customer base. The real clientele are premium business travelers, families, and travelers going for celebratory splurges, she says.

"If you fly from LA to New York and back in first class, these days, that's around $4,000. If you do that private, that's probably $100,000,” Porter explains. “The gap is so big, and there are many people that want to bridge that."

For the last decade, PS has continued to expand. After renaming itself to PS in 2020, it opened a terminal at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) in 2023. The PS terminal at DFW opened on June 1 and was quickly followed by another PS location at Miami International Airport (MIA) later that month. This October, I flew between the two new terminals to get a better idea of how the exclusive service works behind the scenes—and who it’s actually for.

Each private suite has a bathroom complete with Le Labo products, plush towels, and robes.

In Porter’s view, departing is the most stressful part of air travel. "That's when you're asking, 'Where am I going? What time is my plane? Where's my gate?'" she says. Arrivals or transfers can be just as confusing for many travelers: going through immigration and customs, dealing with heavy bags, finding the right taxi stand or connecting to the right terminal for the next flight. The point of PS is to make both legs of the airport journey as seamless as possible.

After I was welcomed at the PS facility at Dallas-Fort Worth and spent a night in the city, I experienced the departure product en route to Miami. I once again rolled up in a chauffeured car to the PS terminal, where caviar was (naturally) waiting for me. The Dallas terminal occupies a gated facility adjacent to Corporate Aviation at DFW and was designed by interior designer Jean Liu to feel residential, like a luxury hotel.

The 40-foot bar in “The Salon” at the Dallas PS terminal.

I spent much of my pre-flight time in the public lounge area dubbed “the Salon,” which had floor-to-ceiling windows looking out over the tarmac. This area hosts a stunning 40-foot bar, taking inspiration from an old-fashioned Southern saloon. Once I settled in, I ordered breakfast (in Dallas, PS executive chef Matt Roman's blue cornbread is a must), and then worked and read a magazine. My boarding pass came with a sheet telling me when to be ready to board, though the PS staff guides make sure you are always where you need to be regardless.

Behind the scenes, the Control Room tracks all flights, delays, arrivals, and departures. From there, PS coordinates with the airline, TSA, and Customs and Border Protection, and stays in direct contact with the flight crews, which is how they’ll know your flight is delayed before the passengers at the gate do.

When it was time for me to board, I went through security right inside the PS terminal. It's a real TSA checkpoint, because PS is the only company in the United States with a private partnership with both TSA and CBP. Guests go through one at a time, and if you check a bag, PS checks it in with the airline for you. Once again, a car drove me to my plane, and I walked up a set of steps outside the jet bridge, through a door, and straight to my seat.

The open-air courtyard at the Miami PS terminal, located in the historic Pan Am headquarters.

By the time I got to Miami, I knew the PS drill. A sign with my name on it waited at the jet bridge, and from the plane it was a 15-minute drive to the original Pan Am headquarters.

At 34,000 square feet, the PS terminal in Miami is nearly three times the size of the one in Dallas—and the design could not be more different. That’s because the Miami terminal is a loving restoration: the building once housed both Pan Am's former headquarters and its stewardess college, where flight attendants trained in the 1960s. In March 2026, the buildings were added to the National Register of Historic Places as part of the “Pan American Airways Historic District," making the terminal a stunning architectural gem.

Pan Am’s Miami headquarters first opened in 1964, sat empty for 15 years, and was slated for demolition before PS restored it. The restoration shows off the New Formalist style (the bold, geometric designs of Miami's postwar resort boom), with an exterior wrapped in a patterned concrete screen and a repeating trapezoid design that reappears in the planters and door handles. The original insignias and gold paneling are still there, and going up the stairs, the Pan Am logo is engraved over and over into the stone wall.

The Miami PS terminal is filled with playful vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers.

Within the terminal, each PS suite has a different vibe (mine was pink), complete with nods to the beach and vintage touches, including palm tree wallpaper and capiz shell chandeliers. The courtyard is open-air, with a decorative pool tiled by Miami artist Nina Surel in Art Deco pastels that's lined with pink-and-white striped loungers and fringed umbrellas. This time, my Private Suite opened onto a balcony overlooking the courtyard. Inside was the same selection of amenities as in Dallas, plus a fresh food menu that was fitting for glitzy Miami: sashimi with cilantro dust, the classic caviar and Champagne, and—for good measure—a cubano. I enjoyed a chair massage, one of the spa's 30-minute treatments (including reflexology, manicures, hair and beard trims, and full-body massages). As much as I would have liked to linger, when it was time to go I took a sandwich to-go for my next flight, and left in PS style: Another car. Another plane.

Of course, none of this comes cheap. PS operates on a tiered membership system: The entry-level Salon Membership costs $1,250 annually, puts access to the Salon at $995 per person, and allows a member to book a Private Suite (accommodating up to four travelers) for $4,950. The top-tier All Access Membership is priced at $4,850 per year, and lowers access rates to the Salon to $895 per person, and Private Suite rates to $3,650. Without a membership, entry to the Salon costs $1,295 per person, and a Private Suite booking costs $4,950. Notably, because the Salon has an age requirement (21 and over, there’s alcohol), parties traveling with those underage are required to book a Private Suite. Pets are welcome in all PS private terminals, and all PS reservations must be made at least 24 hours ahead of travelers’ departure times.

Access to the private suites starts at $4,950 for members, with room for four travelers.

How should you decide if it's a worthwhile purchase for your trip? Porter is honest about which travelers should skip the whole thing: “If you're on your own, with no checked bags, going on an hour flight for the weekend, then the airport is just fine,” she says. "It makes the most sense for long flights and complicated routings; and parties with a lot of checked bags, kids, and older parents who could use the assistance.”

Because the concept blends private and commercial aviation in a way that hasn't been done before, Porter believes it's hard for travelers to fully understand the value of PS—until they've experienced it themselves. "It's just complete peace of mind," she tells me in Dallas. “That's what we're selling.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6337. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6336. Review: KLM 787-10 Business Class (Amsterdam – Los Angeles), Still A Solid Choice

I don’t need an airline to surprise me every time. Sometimes I want to know what I’m getting. My KLM 787-10 business class flight from Amsterdam to Los Angeles reminded me why I keep choosing KLM…and why I still wish it would turn down the heat!

I recently flew KLM’s Boeing 787-10 in World Business Class from Amsterdam to Los Angeles once again, about a year after the flight reviewed below. The seat and overall experience have changed little, so I’ll offer a more abbreviated review of my latest flight. My comprehensive review follows, with a detailed look at the cabin and seat features. In short: nothing has changed at KLM, for better or for worse.

Yes, especially for 60,000 Flying Blue miles (though I’d probably now pay the extra to get out of “light” class). The seat was comfortable and the food was excellent. I enjoyed the flight even though I knew almost exactly what to expect.

The warm cabin remains my biggest complaint, particularly because I encountered the same issue on this route last year. Individual air vents would help accommodate those of us who prefer a cooler sleeping environment.

Even so, this was a comforting way to get home to Los Angeles. Familiar and even boring does not have to mean disappointing.

The detailed review below covers my April 2025 flight on the same aircraft type and route. It includes more detailed info on the seat features, inflight entertainment, Wi-Fi, lavatories, and amenity kit.

My 11-hour KLM flight from Amsterdam to Los Angeles on the 787-10 in World Business Class was smooth, comfortable, but a little warm…

I’ve reviewed the KLM A330, 777, and 787-9 in business class and also the 787-10 in economy class, but this was my first time flying the 787-10 in business class.

I arrived at the KLM Crown Lounge quite early to get my work done for the day, just in case the internet did not function on my flight. While the lounge gets crowded, I quite like it.

Boarding began at 9:05, 45 minutes before departure.

I entered via door 2L and proceeded through the galley and turned left to my seat in 4K.

The KLM 787-10 business class cabin features 38 Jamco America Venture seats arranged in a 1-2-1 reverse herringbone configuration. These Japanese-made seats are 10-15% lighter than traditional reverse herringbone seats.

Seat pitch is generous and seats convert into a fully lie-flat bed (75 inches long). There’s a side storage compartment, seat controls on the armrest, two USB-A ports (one on the side and one under the screen), and a universal power outlet.

My left armrest could be raised (for use when seated) and lowered (to give more space for sleeping).

Interestingly, I noticed the seat looked a bit tattered…at least cosmetically. The paint was chipped on the armrest and under the monitor and the (faux) leather shell around the seat was discolored. There was also noticeable dirt and grime. Everything functioned, but it really looked like an old product, even though my aircraft, PH-BKG, was only delivered five years ago.

Bedding on KLM is comparatively average, with a large pillow and soft duvet-style blanket. There is no day blanket or mattress pad.

I tried to sleep after lunch but the cabin was warm and there were no personal air vents. I did manage a few hours of sleep, but I would have loved to sleep eight hours…a cool cabin and a plush mattress pad would have helped.

The retrofitted 777 World Business Class cabins offer suites with closing doors; the 787-10 do not have this extra feature.

The 11-hour journey to California included lunch after takeoff, a midflight snack, and a meal before landing. Menus were waiting on each seat and KLM continues to print menus for each flight (you’ll notice on the backside of the menu lists your flight number and flight date).

Pre-departure beverages were offered before takeoff, including beer, sparkling wine, orange juice, and “Royal Blue Legend,” the KLM signature cocktail with lemon, ginger, and spirulina…which I had to try.

Lunch began after takeoff, with a refreshing amuse bouche (I don’t even know what it was, but the green thing was topped in a toasted walnut and was very nice) and a drink (I enjoyed “The Very High Fashioned” cocktail, a riff on an Old Fashioned).

I had chili shrimps with pickled watermelon and beetroot mousse and fresh watercress for my appetizer…a great collection of flavors. I was served with a small green salad and bread with Dutch butter. I switched to a Boschendal Boschen Blane 2023 (white wine from South Africa).

For my main course, I chose salmon à la Flamande with Hollandaise sauce, served with white asparagus, scrambled eggs, and potatoes. The salmon filet was very small, but it was a good choice.

For dessert, cheese (blue cheese and Beemster Royaal Fenugreek cheese) with crackers, grapes, and a raisin salad with pine nuts, followed by a tart raspberry mousse topped with sunflower seeds, topped with passion fruit crumble.

About halfway through the flight, passengers were offered a vegetarian croquette sandwich with mustard (I tried that) or a mini club sandwich. Both were served with cherry cheesecake ice cream, which I skipped.

A self-serve station was also set up in the galley with Dutch snacks:

105 minutes before landing, a Caesar salad with pulled chicken, egg, tomatoes, Reypenaar cheese, and pine nuts was offered along with a side of pumpkin ravioli in cream artichoke sauce. A very nice pre-arrival meal, though the pasta was served wrapped in aluminum foil…that could have easily been removed.

The internet worked well on the flight (the flight pass was €22) and it turned out to be a very productive flight when it became clear I could not sleep.

I also managed one movie on the flight, an old Brad Pitt, Kevin Spacey, and Morgan Freeman film called Seven. A little jarring, to say the least…

The KLM IFE library includes music, movies, TV shows, games, and a moving flight map.

KLM’s 787-10 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin reserved for business class passengers (and also for crew use). As always on KLM, I appreciate the tulip flower and the Delft Blue House wallpaper. Soap products were from Marie-Stella-Maris.

The amenity kit also had products from Marie-Stella-Maris (face cream and lip balm) and also included socks, a pen, earplugs, and a dental kit (with tootpaste tablets instead of a tube of toothpaste).

As we approached LAX, the purser came around with Delft Blue Houses, the signature “souvenir” of KLM World Business Class. I was hoping for house 98, which was the parental home of Anthony Fokker in Haarlem (Fokker went on to become one of the world’s greatest aircraft builder in the late 1920’s with factories in the Netherlands and the USA) and I got it!

Then the lady in front of me did not want a house, so I asked if I could have hers and got a second one, 89.

The crew was very seasoned/mature (as always on KLM, it seems) and also very lovely. Very attentive service with a smile and I appreciated so much that flight attendants roamed the cabin throughout the flight, not just during the formal meal services.

It was a beautiful morning (yes, still morning) when we landed at LAX 11 hours later and we flew right over downtown LA and the iconic In-N-Out next to LAX.

KLM offers a very average business class, which is to say a very solid business class. I enjoyed good service, great food, and a comfortable seat on the flight, though the lack of air vent and warm cabin made sleeping difficult. I like the 787-10 and look forward to flying KLM again.

#6335. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6334. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6333. Why The Pilatus PC-24 Can Land On Grass Runways Most Private Jets Cannot

Park a typical business jet beside a wet grass strip, and its crew will probably look for another airport. A jet engine inhales air at tremendous speed, so a loose stone or a splash of mud can turn a routine landing into a six-figure repair. But one Swiss twinjet has been formally approved to do exactly what its rivals avoid. According to Pilatus, the Pilatus PC-24 is certified for takeoffs and landings on grass, wet soil, dry sand, gravel, and snow-covered unpaved runways.

That sounds like a brochure line until you read the certification record. The real question is not whether a PC-24 can touch down on turf once, in perfect weather, but how Pilatus convinced regulators to approve it as normal operation. The answer involves a flooded English field, a snowy test site in northern Canada, a specific main-wheel pressure, and a design decision taken years before the first prototype flew. But first, why do almost all of its rivals stay on the pavement?

The short answer is that they were built that way on purpose. As we explained here, most business jets are optimized for efficiency, speed, and comfort on paved runways, while unpaved operations demand reinforced landing gear and specialized tires that add weight. Modifying a finished design to cope would be expensive and impractical. We also noted that turbofans are less forgiving than propeller aircraft when it comes to foreign object damage, the industry term for debris sucked into an engine.

Grass adds problems that pavement never poses. A wet turf strip can lengthen braking distances, ruts and soft patches can punish the nose and main gear, and a hidden stone is invisible from the cockpit. For a pilot of a conventional jet, every one of those variables is a reason to divert. For an engineer, each one is a design requirement that must be met before the first landing, not after.

There are exceptions, but they come with asterisks. According to the same report, the Dassault Falcon 20 and Falcon 50 can land on dirt and gravel after being fitted with a special service bulletin kit, yet neither was originally designed for it. The PC-24 started from the opposite direction. Pilatus says the jet was developed for rough-field use from the outset, a mindset inherited from its PC-12 turboprop, and the company markets it as the “Super Versatile Jet.” That distinction matters more than it sounds. A jet that can be coaxed onto a grass strip by a brave crew is one thing; a jet whose manufacturer has proven the maneuver to aviation authorities is another. So what did that proof actually look like?

It took two stages. Pilatus first obtained certification for dry sand and gravel in 2018, then spent all of 2019 on a post-certification test campaign. In a media release dated February 7, 2020, the company announced full rough-field approval, adding grass, wet soil, and snow-covered unpaved runways. As reported by AOPA in its coverage of the PC-24's expanded rough-field certification, European regulators approved the aircraft's expanded unpaved-runway capabilities, with US approval following. This gave the eight-seat jet access to a much wider network of airports. According to Pilatus' own technical brochure, the PC-24 can access almost twice as many airports worldwide as competing business jets, thanks largely to its ability to operate from unpaved runways.

The EASA requires certification tests to be flown on different surfaces, so Pilatus took the jet across two continents. Business Jet Traveler listed the grass-runway sites as Goodwood and Duxford in England, Kunovice in the Czech Republic and Poitiers in France. According to our previous report, engineers also flooded an English field with about 45,000 US gallons (170,000 liters) of water to mimic rain of roughly 0.16 inches (4 mm) per hour, and the PC-24 coped. In the Czech Republic, crews rehearsed single-engine take-offs, engine failures and the loss of ground spoilers and anti-skid, with heavy rain adding to the challenge.

Wet soil was arguably the hardest case. Pilatus says the Woodbridge site in England required complex conditions to be reproduced in part, just to meet every specification for take-offs and landings on wet dirt. The company also took the jet to Kuujjuaq, Canada, for snow-covered gravel, a surface where visibility, drag and braking all change at once.

Passing a braking test was only part of the job. Engineers also wanted to know what the surface did to the airplane: whether snow packed into the flaps, whether stones reached the engines, whether brakes and steering held up. Nothing was ingested by the engines and the jet performed better than expected. Which raises the obvious follow-up: what did Pilatus build into the aircraft to make that possible?

The Pilatus PC-24 is a popuar and capable jet from the Swiss manufacturer. Here are 8 top facts.

The PC-24 uses long-stroke trailing-link landing gear that smooths out uneven ground, and its main tires run at 73-76.5 psi (5-5.24 bar) so the aircraft does not sink into soft surfaces. A trailing link hangs each wheel from a pivoting arm, so the wheel can rise and fall over a bump without hammering the airframe. The logic behind the tire pressure is the same as snowshoes: lower pressure spreads weight across a larger footprint, which matters when the aircraft weighs up to 18,700 pounds (8,500 kg) at takeoff.

Then comes the engine problem. The two Williams FJ44-4A turbofans, each producing about 3,400 pounds of thrust (15 kN), sit high on the rear fuselage, far from the stones and spray the wheels throw up. The same report adds that the wing flaps shield the engines from debris. During the Canadian trials, one prototype carried instrumentation and cameras to show whether snow or slush built up on the flaps, fuselage or landing gear, so engineers could compare the impact with dry gravel.

Braking was a separate question. According to our previous report, Pilatus asked whether steering was affected, whether the brakes were sufficient, and how the anti-skid system behaved on loose surfaces. Those details determine whether a crew can stop a fast, heavy aircraft on a surface that gives way underfoot, and we checked them through inspections and recorded data rather than assuming them. Rugged feet are only half of a rough-field jet. The other half is the wing, and it hides the most counterintuitive trick in the design. How does an airplane that cruises at 440 knots arrive so slowly?

A jet capable of cruising at 440 knots might seem an unlikely candidate for short, unimproved runways. Yet that combination of speed and short-field performance is precisely what sets the Pilatus PC-24 apart. Much of the credit goes to its large double-slotted flap system, which Simple Flying credits with delivering the performance the aircraft needs. Pilatus lists a take-off distance of 3,090 feet (942 meters), and our specification list puts the landing distance at 2,410 feet (734 meters) over a 50-foot (15-meter) obstacle, both measured on a dry paved runway at sea level. At the other end of the envelope, Pilatus says the PC-24 cruises at 440 knots (506 miles per hour, or 815 km per hour) and flies up to 2,000 nautical miles (2,301 miles, or 3,704 km).

The aircraft's capabilities are not just theoretical. Simple Flying reports that in an interview conducted with Ashley Fredricks, the first woman to fly the PC-24, one memorable stop was at Valemount, British Columbia. The airport had no control tower, no fuel facilities, and a runway measuring just 3,900 feet (1,200 meters). Fredricks said the jet did not need the entire runway to land or take off. After the stop, the crew flew directly to San Jose, California, more than 1,100 miles (1,770 km) away.

That combination of jet speed and short-field flexibility makes the PC-24 more than an unusual aircraft specification. It also raises a practical question: who is actually buying a jet capable of operating from dirt strips?

The PC-24 has been produced by Pilatus since 2018.

In the 2020 announcement, Pilatus chairman Oscar Schwenk said the Royal Flying Doctor Service of Australia, along with operators in North America and Africa, already used rough-field runways on a regular basis. For an air ambulance serving the outback, landing close to the patient instead of at a distant paved airport can change the whole timeline.

The newest example is Indonesia. According to a Pilatus release dated March 30, 2026, the Indonesian Ministry of Defense signed for twelve PC-24s to support pilot training, air transport and liaison missions. Pilatus says the jet’s ability to use short and unpaved runways, which improves access to remote islands in a nation of 17,000 of them, was a decisive selection criterion.

Pilatus adds that the PC-24 is certified for single-pilot operation and carries a standard cargo door, which makes it useful for training and liaison flights as well as passengers. That combination, a jet that can carry freight, fly with one pilot and still reach a small strip, is exactly what a government fleet looks for when its territory is mostly water and small runways.

Both of those buyers are betting that the capability will keep mattering. The open question is whether any rival will spend the years of testing needed to challenge it, and that question shapes everything that follows.

The significance goes beyond one aircraft. Because certification is evidence rather than marketing, the PC-24’s rough-field approval works as a barrier: a competitor would need to repeat a multi-site, multi-surface campaign like the one Pilatus flew across England, the Czech Republic, France and Canada before making the same claim. A manufacturer cannot bolt that credential on after the fact. There is also a quieter commercial effect.

Pilatus says the PC-24 reaches almost twice as many airports as competing business jets, and every extra airport is another destination without a car transfer, a second flight, or a long drive. For an owner, that can turn a three-hour road trip into a short hop. For an operator, it widens the customer base for anyone whose business sits far from a major runway.

The clearest test will be the order book. Pilatus had delivered 100 PC-24s by the end of 2020, and the Indonesian contract shows government buyers now cite unpaved capability as a deciding factor. If more air forces, air ambulance services and remote-region operators follow that logic, the grass strip stops being a curiosity and starts being a market. One caution belongs here. Certification describes what the aircraft is approved to do, not a promise that every field is good, so crews still judge each strip on the day. The question to see is which other jet will be certified to follow it.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
