#6321. 5 Qantas Boeing 787-9 Routes Longer Than 8,000 Miles

Leena Robinson | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Qantas runs the most demanding Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner network in the world today. Five routes flown by the airline's Dreamliners stretch beyond 8,000 miles, and the longest of them, Perth to London, has needed a Singapore fuel stop westbound since Middle East airspace closures forced longer flight paths. This countdown ranks the five by great circle distance, from Perth to Rome at about 8,300 miles (13,357 km) up to Perth to London at 9,010 miles (14,500 km).

The jet's originally published range is 8,706 miles (14,010 km), and by simple conversion four of the five routes exceed it. Qantas closes the gap by flying only 236 seats on each aircraft, according to Airways, roughly 50 fewer than a typical two-class layout, and by building schedules around the wind. This countdown examines how the Dreamliner successfully redefined the iconic Kangaroo Route thanks to the ultra-long-haul 787-9.

Qantas flight QF5 took off from Perth on the night of June 22, 2022. Qantas had not flown to Rome since 2003, back when it operated multi-stop Boeing 747 services via cities like Singapore and Bangkok. While initially launched in response to surging post-pandemic summer holiday crowds, the business profile of QF5/QF6 has evolved into a highly resilient asset.

The route covers about 8,300 miles (13,357 km), and the westbound leg lasts 16 hours and 25 minutes. It is roughly 700 miles (1,126 km) shorter than Perth to London, and thus is the only route on this list that allows the 787-9 to carry a truly full load of passengers and cargo. QF5 has also remained fully nonstop in both directions despite other long-haul itineraries being forced to use layovers since Russia closed its airspace in 2022.

The flying season spans roughly six months from Spring to Fall and, thanks to exceptional demand, the service has carried well over 70,000 passengers since its inception. Qantas relies on connections in Perth to allow travelers from the east coast of Australia to step off a domestic flight and board a Rome-bound Dreamliner. More than 50% of the route’s passengers come from Australia's eastern cities: Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane.

The Auckland (AKL) to New York (JFK) corridor is one of the most intensely contested and economically vital battlegrounds in modern ULH aviation. It operates over a distance of 8,828 miles (14,207 km). Historically, traffic connecting Australia and New Zealand to the East Coast of the US relied on multi-stop journeys via West Coast gateways like Los Angeles (LAX) or San Francisco (SFO). Today, the route operates as a fierce, high-stakes duopoly between Qantas (QF3/QF4) and its cross-Tasman rival, Air New Zealand (NZ2/NZ1).

Air New Zealand initially pioneered the nonstop air bridge in 2022. Qantas launched New York flights on June 14, 2023, after a gap of more than three years, using Auckland as the stop in place of LAX, meeting Air New Zealand head-on. Spanning nearly 14,200 kilometers, the flight time regularly stretches between 16 hours and 17.5 hours, heavily dictated by severe high-altitude jet streams shifting across the Pacific Ocean. This extreme distance places intense operational constraints on Qantas’ 787-9.

Perth Airport (PER) – Rome Fiumicino Airport (FCO)

Auckland Airport (AKL) – John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK)

Perth Airport (PER) – Paris Charles De Gaulle Airport (CDG)

Melbourne Airport (MEL) – Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW)

Perth Airport (PER) – London Heathrow Airport (LHR)

Data shows that only 33% of the flight’s total passenger load originates in Sydney. The remaining two-thirds of the cabin is dynamically fed by passengers funneling from other Australian hubs, predominantly Brisbane and Melbourne, alongside local New Zealand flyers. The route relies heavily on top-tier premium business travel during the week, capturing finance, technology, and corporate executives moving between the financial districts of Sydney, Melbourne, and Manhattan. On weekends, the traffic shifts toward high-end premium leisure travelers.

In order to safely undertake the long trans-Pacific sortie, the 787-9 must trade some of its payload for fuel before taking off. That requires the Qantas business model to maximize appeal to higher-paying customers like business travelers and drop some of its seating capacity in the economy section. It has proven to be a highly lucrative asset, capturing an exceptionally high average load factor of 84% for Qantas. Owing to its popularity, QF3/QF4 operates Monday to Friday with weekend service during surges.

Huge changes are coming to Qantas' longest services. See them all here!

Qantas began nonstop flying from Perth to Paris in July 2024, making history by establishing the first nonstop twinjet service between Australia and France. Australian Aviation reported that the inaugural QF33 flight was scheduled for 17 hours and 20 minutes. The route covers 8,863 miles (14,263 km), a little shorter than London but well past the 787-9's full payload range.

The route immediately injected 75,000 annual seats into the Europe–Australia market. Prior to this service, Qantas had not touched down in the French capital since 2004, when it retired its aging Boeing 747-400 multi-stop service via Singapore. In the years that passed, like its sister route to London (QF9), the Perth–Paris sector has become a major case study in adapting to complex international geopolitics.

In response to volatile Middle East airspace closures, Qantas had to dynamically reroute flights to ensure absolute passenger safety. While the route was initially engineered to be a strict nonstop, Qantas shifted its operational strategy for the westbound Perth-to-Paris leg to include a technical and commercial stopover at Singapore Changi Airport (SIN). Rather than treating the Singapore detour as a pure operational penalty, Qantas masterfully converted it into a commercial victory.

QF33 relies on capturing top-tier 'Kangaroo Route' market share away from Middle Eastern airlines. By permanently re-routing the service via Singapore, Qantas expanded overall Paris network frequencies from three weekly flights up to five. Exactly like the Rome service, this flight officially originates at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD), but concurrently, Qantas boosted feeder flights between Perth and Singapore. The air bridge has thrived in spite of obstacles and commands premium prices from travelers eager to avoid a middle-of-the-night stopover in the Gulf.

After a decade of planning, Qantas is finally set to begin its groundbreaking nonstop service between Sydney and London next year.

Melbourne Airport's chief executive called it the longest route ever flown from the city when Qantas started Melbourne to Dallas/Fort Worth flights in December 2022. It was also the fourth longest in the world at the time, according to Airways. The airline framed the mission as a companion to its existing Sydney to Dallas flights, and it even flies the same 787-9 with 236 seats, split into 42 business, 28 premium economy, and 166 economy.

The route covers 7,862 nautical miles, nearly as far as Perth to London, and the schedule shows how much the wind matters. QF21 from Melbourne is scheduled for 16 hours and 10 minutes, while QF22 from Dallas runs 17 hours and 40 minutes because it flies into headwinds across the Pacific. The massive one-and-a-half-hour time difference between the eastbound and westbound flights is caused by high-altitude jet streams. On the return flight, the aircraft faces severe, sustained headwinds.

As one of the longest commercial flight routes in the world, this segment acts as a vital strategic bridge, linking Australia to the heart of American Airlines' network in North America. Melbourne is one of Qantas' strongholds, while DFW is the top mega-hub for AA. This pairing allows the two airlines to function as a single network, harmonizing flight schedules. The route operates on a stable, year-round schedule of four weekly flights with an average load factor of approximately 81.9%.

Airbus' A350-1000ULR begins testing as Project Sunrise moves closer to reality.

The Perth to London Heathrow (QF9/QF10) route is the crown jewel of Qantas’ international network. Covering 9,010 miles (14,500 km), it is Australia’s flagship 'Kangaroo Route' and famously became the first nonstop passenger service between Australia and the United Kingdom when it launched on March 24, 2018. Melbourne Airport also declared that QF9 was the longest route ever flown from the city.

For nearly seven decades, traveling between Australia and Britain required multiple stops, spawning the affectionate nickname for the journey 'down under.' When Qantas deployed the 787-9 Dreamliner to link Western Australia directly with London, it upended the entire concept. Today, travelers are willing to pay an incredible 20% to 30% price premium for a nonstop flight compared to one-stop itineraries from competitors.

The scheduled block time is 17 hours and 30 minutes outbound and 16 hours and 50 minutes on the return. Following volatile Middle East airspace closures, flying entirely nonstop from Perth to London became too fuel-intensive on the outbound leg. Qantas introduced a brief layover in Singapore just as it did on the Paris route in order to overcome the obstacle. Even so, the demand for QF9/QF10 remains robust, with cabins regularly clearing 94% to 95% load factors on a permanent, daily year-round schedule.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6320. American Airlines business class to Prague for just 55,000 points: Here's how you can do it, too

It's not often that you can fly from the U.S. to Europe in business class for just 55,000 points, but sometimes, deals are out there — especially if you use American Airlines AAdvantage miles or Atmos Rewards points.

I found a great award using Atmos Rewards Points on American Airlines' newly resumed nonstop flight from Philadelphia to Prague. As mentioned, I paid just 55,000 points (and $5.60 in taxes and fees).

I'll get into some detail on how to find these kinds of deals, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

I wanted the chance to check American's European service and compare the business-class products on the older 787-8s (like the one I flew to Prague) and the new premium-heavy 787-9P planes I've flown to London.

American Airlines relaunched its Prague service in May of this year. It had previously served the route for a few years, in 2018 and 2019, before abandoning it during the coronavirus pandemic.

AA now operates the route seasonally during the busy summer period, from May to October, between Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) and Václav Havel Airport Prague (PRG). The airline has already said the route will return for summer 2027.

Another good sign for the route: AA is adding more European destinations from Philadelphia next summer, including Vienna and Porto, Portugal. American Airlines calls Prague part of "the airline's Central European network."

I kicked off my journey with a few days in Philadelphia before heading to the airport.

A post shared by Clint Page Henderson (@clintpage1)

American Airlines' Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia opened in May of last year, after years of delays. It is a lovely space to spend a few hours before your flight, though it can get crowded at times. I could access it because I was flying long-haul business class.

A great American Airlines agent named Thomas Doersam, who has been with AA for 38 years, gave me a quick tour of the Flagship and the adjacent Admirals Club.

The Flagship lounge (American's fifth) is near Gate A15, where AA's long-haul flights depart. Eligible passengers flying long-haul business class can use the Flagship Lounge, which includes those in business class on these flights.

Others have access to the Admiral's Club just across the way.

It has been lovely to see American Airlines invest so much in its lounge product. In fact, a sixth Flagship lounge was announced for Charlotte, along with a massive new Admiral's Club that will clock in at more than 40,000 square feet.

I had seat 1L on this 11-year-old Boeing 787 Dreamliner, with the ship number N806AA. This is a legacy interior that will eventually be phased out.

TPG reported that these planes will receive new Flagship business-class suites and a full cabin refresh, though AA didn't say when that would start.

I was on the smallest Dreamliner variant, and the business-class cabin had just 20 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration. All the seats had aisle access.

These lie-flat seats were 21 inches wide and featured American's version of the Safran Concept D seat (formerly known as Zodiac).

I found them to be fairly comfortable, if a bit narrow, during the overnight journey.

Some flyers complain about these seats since some are rear-facing. The seats are attached to each other, and some people say they feel it when the person seated next to them moves. (Some flyers even refer to them as "rocking chairs.") It never bothered me on my previous trips in these seats, and it didn't this time either, even though I was in the first row.

There were also 28 premium economy seats on this plane — a comfortable and potentially more affordable option.

There were also 186 economy seats, including 48 Main Cabin Extra seats.

Inflight entertainment was provided by a 15-inch screen that could pop out with the push of a button. There were plenty of shows and movies to choose from.

Still, these screens are showing their age, especially now that more innovative 4K screens are rolling out across many fleets (including American's).

Inflight Wi-Fi was provided by Panasonic and cost $35 for the full flight. It was just OK, and I was glad I wasn't relying on it for important work. American Airlines will begin rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, but in the meantime, representatives say there are plans to improve Wi-Fi speeds on its 787s, too. I expect the overall tech picture to improve dramatically over the next few years.

The airlines have had some pretty major connection problems recently.

Remember, these seats are a decade old and show a bit of wear and tear. Still, it's a comfortable cabin, and because there are so few business-class seats, it does feel a bit special.

My seat had plenty of other bells and whistles that I won't go into too much detail here, but I appreciated the overhead air vents and some of the nooks and crannies for storing items.

I also loved American's newer bedding. The zipper bag held a large blanket and pillow; mattress pads were also available at each seat. While it may not look as fancy as United's Saks bedding, I found it super comfortable.

Amenity kits were made in honor of the World Cup, featuring a clear design filled with standard amenities.

You can read more details about the hard product on these planes in the reviews linked above, but I think, in general, I'm a bigger fan than most when it comes to the seats on these Dreamliners.

As I mentioned, I don't mind the older 787s, but there's no question: American's new 787Ps are a fresher product.

TPG's Eric Rosen and I reviewed the new product last year, and we were both pretty impressed. AA unveiled its all-new Flagship Suite business class in May, and Eric and I were eager to experience the new planes and try out the Flagship Suite Preferred and Flagship Suite business-class seats. He took a flight from London to Chicago, and I was flying from Chicago to London.

Unlike the 787-8s, which have just 20 business-class seats, the new 787Ps have a whopping 51 Flagship Suites.

It will be interesting to see whether AA expands the business-class and premium-class cabins during the retrofit of these planes.

You can really see the differences in the photos below.

Aside from the size of the business-class cabin, the biggest difference is the sliding doors on the 787Ps.

There are eight Flagship Suite Preferred seats on the 787Ps — an upgraded version of the new suites with additional space.

Finally, the new 787Ps have updated designs, more storage, a lounger mode on the seat controls, wireless charging and dramatically better 17.3-inch IFE screens with both Bluetooth and touchscreen capability.

While I love the new planes, I wouldn't choose a more expensive redemption just to fly them.

I had a great crew on my flight to Prague, with friendly service and generally good food and beverage.

Not only did we get a predeparture beverage, but service was prompt, friendly and efficient.

Dinner started with warmed nuts and a beverage of your choice. Appetizers included a small romaine salad, along with citrus-poached shrimp and ceviche-style fish. For a main course, I finally tried American Airlines' new "sliders and fries." It was only available as a pre-order, but I'm so glad I took the time to select it because it was delicious.

Dessert was the classic sundae which I ordered with extra whipped cream. How can you resist?

Breakfast was yogurt with granola and fruit that AA calls a "fresh fruit bowl" — perfectly fine for an airplane breakfast. The best part was the multiple cappuccinos I drank. (American brought back espresso drinks in business class in 2025, and I've made full use of the perk.)

I even received a thank-you note from my flight attendant, Daniel — a rare and lovely touch that I don't often find with U.S. airlines.

As I mentioned, I scored my business-class seat for just 55,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in taxes and fees. Remember, you can book American Airlines flights using Alaska points, and it can often be an even better deal.

Related: Why American Airlines AAdvantage has become my most valuable rewards currency

Often, when a new route is launched or resumed, you'll see airlines make award tickets more available than usual. That's just what happened here, when the airline made business-class redemptions on both Prague and its newly resumed Budapest route widely available, even on partners like Alaska.

When a new route starts or an old one resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

To start, flexibility is key. If you can be flexible on dates and destinations, the world literally opens up. Let the deal guide where you go.

Try booking as soon as schedules open up. For carriers like Japan Airlines, you'll find the best availability 11 months in advance, as that's when seats open to partner airlines.

Award search tools have also become a huge part of my process. Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel are my favorites. I also love the award tool Points Path, which sits on my browser, so I see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

American Airlines also has a great tool that I use to find deals. I use the airline's award search calendar to find business-class seats for months at a time. Here's an example of that for flights from New York City to Rome, Paris and Amsterdam for next year.

I wouldn't book any of these because of the high taxes and fees for partner awards, but it at least gives an idea of what's out there.

My last suggestion: Keep checking flights in case the price drops.

Sometimes, it can make sense to lock in a coach redemption and then keep checking to see if business class opens up at a reasonable rate.

If you are willing to be brave, more availability often opens up at the last minute, and you can find some great deals.

#6319. Park Hyatt Riviera Maya Cancun, Brand’s First All-Inclusive, Opens Soon

Want to take advantage of Hyatt Privé benefits, including a room upgrade, complimentary breakfast, a hotel credit, and more, when booking a cash stay? Contact Ford ([email protected]) for more details. He may even be able to help if you already have a stay booked.

In late 2023, Hyatt and Parks Hospitality Holdings announced a collaboration that will expand Hyatt’s footprint in Mexico, with the development of four new properties. If you ask me, the most interesting of these is the new Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, which will also be the brand’s first all-inclusive property.

There’s now an update, as the hotel’s opening date has just been moved forward by a couple of months, and it’s now expected to open in the coming weeks.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya, located in Cancun, Mexico, is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 3, 2026. The hotel was initially supposed to open in 2025, then it started accepting reservations for stays as of February 2027, and now it’s accepting reservations for stays as of late 2026.

Hopefully the current opening date sticks, but if you book in the first several months the hotel is open, don’t be surprised if we see an additional delay, or at least don’t be surprised if not everything is ready.

The 148-key property will have a first-ever concept for the Park Hyatt brand, as it will be all-inclusive. Admittedly this is pretty normal for the Cancun area, but still, it’s noteworthy for a brand like Park Hyatt.

Hyatt has been leaning heavily into the all-inclusive space in recent times, particularly through acquisitions. So while Hyatt has grown massively in terms of its number of all-inclusive brands, it’s surprising to see even a traditionally non all-inclusive brand get this kind of an experience.

I’m generally not a fan of all-inclusives, or at least historically haven’t chosen to vacation at them. However, after my recent Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection cruise, there is something I really enjoyed about not being nickel-and-dimed for everything, given how expensive luxury hospitality has become in so many places.

When it comes to the dining outlets, they’ll include Beach Grill IK’AL (the beachfront restaurant with seafood and Yucatecan flavors), Bruma (the steakhouse), Nutre Kitchen (the all-day dining restaurant), Pool Bar Brisa (the pool bar serving drinks & light snacks), Patisserie Market & Cafe (the coffee shop), Living Room (the lobby bar).

Accommodations will range in size from 559 square feet (52 square meters) to 2,303 square feet (214 square meters), so they’re generously sized, as you’d expect. The decor looks nice enough, but not like anything special.

As you’d expect, the resort will have amenities including several pools, a full-service spa, a gym, and more.

Once open, this adds to a growing number of luxury points hotels in the Cancun area. Just recently we saw the opening of the St. Regis Kanai and Waldorf Astoria Cancun, so it’s nice to see Hyatt’s most luxurious brand also expand to the Cancun area. As a matter of fact, the Park Hyatt will be immediately next to the Waldorf Astoria (which also recently became all-inclusive, as it wasn’t initially).

The Park Hyatt brand is really growing in Mexico right now. We’ve seen the recent opening of the Park Hyatt Los Cabos at Cabo Del Sol, while the Park Hyatt Mexico City is expected to open in early 2027. Beyond that, we also saw the recent opening of the Alila Mayakoba, another good luxury option in the Cancun area.

With the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya now bookable, what are rates like? If paying cash, rooms seem to generally start at around $1,500 per night, but that does include taxes & fees. So it’s obviously very expensive, but given Mexico’s high taxes & fees, it’s actually not quite as crazy as some may have expected.

Then again, I’m not necessarily expecting this to be typical Park Hyatt quality, given the extent to which this is outside the typical Park Hyatt wheelhouse. Oddly, at least as of now, rates seem to be the same whether one or two people are staying, which is unusual for an all-inclusive.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, a hotel credit, and more.

When redeeming points, the hotel follows World of Hyatt’s Category F all-inclusive award chart, which is the most expensive award pricing for all-inclusive properties.

Under Hyatt’s current award chart, the cost is typically 45,000 to 85,000 points per night, and that’s the same whether the room has single or double occupancy.

The Park Hyatt Riviera Maya is now accepting reservations for stays as of December 2026. The hotel is expected to be an all-inclusive, making it the first Park Hyatt property in the world where that’s the case.

It’s awesome to see Hyatt’s luxury expansion in Mexico, as this will be the third Park Hyatt to open in a fairly short time period. However, the Park Hyatt brand is becoming increasingly inconsistent, and I find the all-inclusive pivot to be a bit strange, especially given how many all-inclusive brands Hyatt already has.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Riviera Maya?

It’s one thing to read about an exciting welcome offer and another to see what it can actually do in real life. So when the IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (see rates and fees) launched with a generous limited-time launch offer, I mapped it onto a weekend in New York City with my mom.

The card, now open to applicants, comes with a launch offer of 200,000 bonus points, earned after you spend $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening (apply by Nov. 18, 2026). Beyond the bonus, its benefits include automatic Platinum Elite status and up to $300 per year in food and beverage rewards at IHG Hotels.

But the real question for many IHG fans is how the welcome offer, benefits and earning rates stack up against an actual getaway.

My mom and I recently spent a mother-daughter weekend in New York City, staying two nights at the Kimpton Era Midtown New York and spending Saturday soaking up the city's art and culture. If you’re considering this card, here’s how our trip played out so you can see just how far all of these perks can go.

My mom had not visited New York in a long time, and I wanted to make sure we were right in the middle of the action while also being near great dining and activities. The Kimpton Era Midtown, which opened in early 2026 in a 33-story tower on West 48th Street, proved to be the perfect home base for us. The Theater District was within walking distance, and we were able to grab a quick subway ride uptown to the Met.

Our two-night weekend stay in New York would have cost 64,600 points per night, or 129,200 points total — versus $1,354 (including taxes and fees) if we'd paid cash.

That means the 200,000-point welcome offer would have covered our entire stay, and I would still have 70,800 points left over to put toward a future trip.

One thing to keep in mind: While we only had a weekend, you can plan a longer trip and take advantage of the fourth-night-free benefit (redeem points for three consecutive nights, get the fourth free) to make your points go even further.

Plus, each year on your cardholder anniversary, you get one free night certificate worth up to 60,000 points. If a night costs more than 60,000 points, IHG allows you to top off the additional points you need. For my stay at the Kimpton Era Midtown, I would have only needed an additional 4,600 points to cover one night, which would have been easy to earn as someone who frequently stays at IHG properties.

Nothing makes me feel more like a VIP at an IHG Hotel than my Platinum Elite Status. Cardholders get automatic IHG One Rewards Platinum Elite status for as long as they keep the card. That comes with perks such as room upgrades and early check-in when available.

Thanks to my loyalty, I applied for a Confirmable Suite Upgrade, one of the Milestone Rewards IHG One Rewards members can choose after reaching certain night thresholds in a calendar year. That means we checked in knowing a premium high-floor room with a view of the Empire State Building was waiting for us.

The surprises and delights didn’t end there, though. We were also given a welcome amenity as a thank-you for my status. I had the option to choose between 5,000 bonus points or a welcome beverage. I usually opt for points when I stay with IHG, but since we were celebrating our mother-daughter weekend, we decided to have some fun and treat ourselves to the welcome drinks.

One of the coolest perks on the IHG Premier Select Card is the $300 in annual Food and Beverage Rewards at IHG hotels, issued as a $75 voucher each calendar quarter. So before heading out for a full day of adventuring on Saturday, my mom and I enjoyed an awesome breakfast at Bar Rocco, and the $75 voucher would have covered our entire meal.

It’s important to note that any charges paid with a Food and Beverage Reward don't earn IHG points, but there are also a few other rules worth knowing to get the most out of this perk:

I booked our round-trip nonstop flights from Orlando International Airport (MCO) to LaGuardia Airport (LGA) directly with JetBlue for $422.85 per person. The IHG Premier Select Card offers a $200 statement credit each calendar year when you spend at least $250 on flights booked directly with an airline through Dec. 31, 2027.

Unlike some travel credits that tie you to a single carrier or a booking portal, this one works with any airline as long as you book directly, as I did. Plus, it’s a win-win because the remaining balance can be paid with the IHG Premier Select Card and earn 6 points per dollar since it counts as a travel purchase.

A weekend in New York City goes beyond the hotel stay. The IHG Premier Select Card helps you earn rewards on your flights, hotel stays and everything in between. This card gets you:

And these earning rates worked out well for our trip, right down to the experiences.

We spent Saturday morning at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where admission for the two of us came to $60, and admired works by my personal favorite painter, Claude Monet, and explored the Temple of Dendur.

Our biggest splurge of the weekend, though, was on two tickets to see "Hamilton" at the Richard Rodgers Theatre, totaling $560. This was a real treat because original Broadway cast member Christopher Jackson (George Washington) temporarily rejoined for a limited engagement.

Since the IHG Premier Select Card earns 3 points per dollar on all other purchases, it will help you make the most of those experiences (and your souvenirs) too.

Our mother-daughter New York City weekend getaway is exactly the kind of trip that the new IHG One Rewards Premier Select Card was built for. And the welcome offer is the best way to make the most of it.

Right now, new cardholders can earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening, but this limited-time launch offer is only available to those who apply by Nov. 18, 2026.

Beyond the welcome offer, the card's earning rates and benefits, such as the food and beverage reward and the $200 airline credit, keep the value coming long after you’ve used your points.

So if you stay at IHG hotels even a couple of times a year, then this card will likely be worth your while — and now is the perfect time to apply.

#6317. 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, cedar barrel sauna, pool and ping-pong tables, arcade games, boot warmers

If you’re an avid East Coast skier, you’re likely no stranger to Killington’s buzzy ski resort, home to over 200 ski trails of terrain for any level shredder. This five-bedroom cabin makes a great launchpad for those staying in the area. The amenity-filled gem sits only four minutes away from Killington Resort, and comes with a game room, cedar barrel sauna, and mountain views for days. Use the boot warmers in the closet before hitting the mountain, then leave all your gear in the ski shed for storage once you’ve returned. In the evenings, fire up some food on the patio grill then cozy up around the wood-burning fireplace.

Where to ski: Killington Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: Killington Skyeship Base Lodge, The Lookout Tavern, Killington Village, Gifford Woods State Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, mountain views, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

I’m adding this Vermont gem to my ski bucket list for a dozen different reasons, starting with the fact that the mountain access is second to none: This spruced-up, slopeside penthouse apartment sits steps from the ski lifts, less than just a five-minute walk to Stowe Mountain Resort’s six-passenger Over Easy Gondola. It’s also a 15-minute drive to one of my favorite mountains, Smugglers’ Notch, where the vibes are always high and the terrain is suitable for all kinds of skiers.

Back at “home,” this modern mountain aesthetic will refresh you after a long day on the slopes. A picture-perfect gas fireplace hangs in front of floor-to-ceiling windows that provide mountain views for days. Tasteful pops of color complete the dining space, comfy blankets line the couch, and the small-but-mighty kitchen has all the appliances you might need for cooking dinner.

Where to ski: Stowe Mountain Resort or Smugglers’ NotchThings to do nearby: Stowe Village, Matterhorn, Cliff House Restaurant, Gondola Skyride (to Mount Mansfield’s peak), The Club at Spruce Peak

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, wraparound deck, dining area with grill, mountain views, wood-burning fireplace

Perched 60 feet above New York’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, with a ski (or hiking) trail just across the street, this rental is ideal for a fun-filled New York ski trip not far from the city. In true log cabin fashion, guests can admire the vaulted ceiling made of cedarwood beams, indoor fireplace, and mountain-facing sliding doors which open to a wraparound deck with a firepit. There are odes to nature everywhere, from framed landscape paintings to horns and antlers as wall decor.

The home’s slopeside location is the real draw: As one previous guest wrote in an Airbnb review, “you’ll feel like you’ll have your own backdoor to Hunter Mountain.” While it’s not a true ski-in/ski-out property, the home sits a quick drive or walk away from the Hunter North area, where you can gear up and take off.

Where to ski: Hunter Mountain Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Tannersville, Hunter Mountain Brewery, Ze Burger Wine Bar, Fellow Mountain Cafe

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedroom, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: California king bed, laundry facilities, wood-burning fireplace, patio with private hot tub

This extra-luxurious abode has the look and feel of an upscale hotel—à la The Cloudveil—but it’s actually a private townhouse at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort with three bedrooms that sleep up to seven. While the prime location may be one of the biggest selling points, the decor and design make it even more enticing: The living room, for example, has classic Jackson Hole touches (note the antler chandelier and cozy fireplace), balanced out by light linens and airy textures. You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

Where to ski: Jackson Hole Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: JH Sports (for gear rentals), Teton Village, Moose Creek Quad Chair, Mangy Moose Jackson Hole

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, wood-burning sauna, gas grill, indoor fireplace, kid-friendly amenities, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

Where to ski: Breckenridge Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Hoosier Pass, Peaceful Valley Lodge, Downtown Breckenridge, Boreas Mountain, Quandary Peak, BreckConnect Gondola

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Fully equipped kitchen, mountain views, hot tub, firepit, central location

This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, Montana, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. And Big Sky Resort sits at the top of many Montana itineraries for good reason—especially come wintertime. Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. For one, each of the two bedrooms feature king beds with mattress warmers to keep you cozy during winter nights. Take advantage of the big patio space for stargazing, relaxing in the hot tub, and cooking up some s’mores before heading inside for a movie night. The house can technically host up to eight guests, but it’s more ideal for families or smaller groups. Aside from the two bedrooms, the living room offers one sofa bed and two bunk beds.

Where to ski: Big Sky ResortThings to do nearby: Lone Mountain Ranch, Gallatin Peak, Big Sky Mountain Village, Fan Mountain, Beehive Peak, Madison Base (at Big Sky Resort)

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski out access, hot tub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

When it comes to access to Utah’s renowned slopes and cool ski towns, you can’t get much better than this four-bedroom luxury penthouse. At the base of Park City Mountain, this condo boasts ski-in/ski-out access directly from the mountain's Silver Star lift. Spacious living areas, a chef’s kitchen, a hot tub, and a balcony overlooking the golf course and icy lakes create a refined on-mountain experience. The penthouse’s proximity to both ski runs and downtown makes for a seamless mix—not to mention you’ll be just a 10-minute drive to Deer Valley Resort, accessible from the condo via a free ski shuttle. With bunk beds for families and plenty of lounge areas for après-ski downtime, this Park City gem accommodates groups seeking easy access to slopes in style.

Where to ski: Park City Mountain; Deer Valley ResortThings to do nearby: Kimball Art Center, Old Town Main Street, Creekside Park, Iron Mountain Trailhead, Thaynes Canyon

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, firepit, fully equipped kitchen, game area, in-unit washer and dryer

New Mexico ski trips mean a real change of scenery, and this year there’s an extra reason to have this underrated mountain range on your radar. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. (It’s a great one for beginners, featuring the renowned Heading Home 3.2-mile green run that traverses all the way from the summit to the base.)

This home is only around 100 yards away from that exact ski run, with slope access right out the door. Inside, there’s a ton of space to sprawl out and indulge in simple creature comforts: soaking in the hot tub, roasting marshmallows around the firepit on the expansive deck, and playing board games (or one of the vintage arcade games inside the den).

Where to ski: Angel Fire Resort; Taos Ski ValleyThings to do nearby: Oeste Vista Trail, Summit Haus, Cabin at Southwest Flyer Lift, Liberation Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound deck, sauna, firepit, unique design, opt-in grocery delivery, Koyo massage chair

Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

Where to ski: Mammoth Mountain Ski AreaThings to do nearby: Twin Lakes Vista, Mammoth Creek Park, Sherwin Lakes Trailhead, Mammoth Brewing Company, Canyon Lodge, Whitmore Hot Springs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside and central location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

Where to ski: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort; Aspen Snowmass Ski Resort; Aspen Highlands Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Where to ski: Big Sky Ski ResortThings to do nearby Lone Mountain Ranch, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center, Gondola Mid Station, Montana Jack, Beehive Basin Trailhead

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

Read more about how El Niño is impacting ski resorts here.

#6316. Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways Sale: Save Up To 50% On Award Flights

Alaska Atmos Rewards offers the Global Getaways promotion, whereby members can save on award tickets in select regions. Atmos Rewards launches this promotion on the first Wednesday of each month (which the program calls “Atmos Members Day”), so we just saw the one for November launched.

Let’s go over the opportunities, as you can save up to 50% on award tickets. There are some cool markets in which you can save miles, though unfortunately only economy travel qualifies.

For the new Alaska Atmos Rewards Global Getaways promotion, you can save up to 50% on award travel to nine destinations, with the following restrictions:

The theme for this Global Getaways promotion is “lights, camera, departure,” with the idea being to “roll out the red carpet for the destinations that have starred in your favorite films and shows.” With this sale, you can save on one-way redemptions to the following destinations (these savings are up to 50%, but not always that high):

I very much appreciate Alaska Atmos Rewards’ creativity with this promotion, as nowadays it’s pretty rare to see programs offer award sales that are also valid for travel on partner airlines. Now, admittedly I wish there weren’t quite as many restrictions in terms of the booking window, travel period, the class of service limitations, and the one-way discount, but still, there will be value here for some, and it’s better than nothing.

If you’re simply looking for the lowest cost award, some of these award prices are very tough to beat. For example, getting from the mainland to Hawaii for 11,500 points is a great deal, as is getting from the United States to India for 30,000 points. Keep in mind that with Atmos Rewards, award flights even earn status points, so could help you qualify for status.

I do hope that over time we see some first and business class award sales as well (it’s probably not happening, but we can dream, right?). Many of us have historically loved the program for the value it offers for premium cabin travel, so this promotion doesn’t help us much with that.

This is basically Alaska’s version of Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards or Singapore KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes, except it applies for travel on partner airlines (rather than just for travel on the program’s airline), and is exclusive to economy (while the other promotions are mixed).

Alaska Atmos Rewards has launched its latest Global Getaways promotion, which is a monthly redemption deal offering up to a 50% discount on awards. This time around, you can save points on economy redemptions to select destinations. You need to book by November 7, 2026, mostly for travel in early 2027. While this won’t be useful for everyone, I imagine some people will get value from this.

What do you make of Alaska’s Global Getaways promotion?

#6315. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

#6314. Why The Boeing 747-400 Was A Turning Point For Two-Pilot Cockpits

Vytautas Kielaitis | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

For almost two decades, operating the Boeing 747 meant having three people on the flight deck. Alongside the captain and first officer, a dedicated flight engineer monitored the jumbo jet's complex systems, managed fuel distribution, checked engine parameters, and ensured its electrical, hydraulic, and pneumatic systems operated correctly. But the introduction of the 747-400 changed this longstanding arrangement, demonstrating that even one of the world's largest commercial aircraft could be operated by just two pilots.

However, the 747-400 was not the first commercial aircraft to adopt a two-pilot cockpit. Boeing 757 and 767 had already demonstrated the advantages of computerized flight decks, while other manufacturers had experimented with similar arrangements on four-engine aircraft. Nevertheless, the 747-400 represented a major milestone in bringing two-pilot operations to the jumbo-jet category. How did Boeing eliminate the flight engineer, what happened to the responsibilities previously assigned to that position, and how did the change influence subsequent generations of commercial aircraft?

When the original Boeing 747 entered commercial service with Pan American World Airways on January 22, 1970, its flight deck reflected late-1960s technology. The aircraft was considerably more complex than previous commercial jetliners, featuring four engines, extensive fuel systems, multiple hydraulic circuits, and sophisticated environmental controls. As a result, Boeing designed the original 747-100 to operate with three flight deck crew members: a captain, a first officer, and a flight engineer. This arrangement continued with the subsequent 747-200 and 747-300 generations. Boeing's official 747 historical overview identifies these three aircraft as the original Classics generation.

On most aircraft, the flight engineer sat in a dedicated seat behind the two pilots, facing a large instrument panel with hundreds of switches, gauges, indicators, and circuit breakers. While the captain and first officer concentrated on flying, navigation, and communication, the flight engineer monitored the aircraft's technical condition and performed numerous operational tasks. This included checking engine performance, managing fuel transfers between tanks, monitoring electrical generators, maintaining hydraulic pressure, and controlling cabin pressurization. On a four-engine aircraft as large as the 747, these responsibilities created a considerable workload, especially during departure, cruise, and abnormal operating conditions. The Boeing 747 flight deck historical overview compares the original cockpit arrangement with its modern successor.

Importantly, the flight engineer was not an additional pilot. The position required specialist technical training and a detailed understanding of aircraft systems, allowing the two pilots to concentrate on their primary flying responsibilities. The arrangement was also common across earlier generations of four-engine commercial aircraft, including the Boeing 707 and Douglas DC-8. However, as electronic systems became more sophisticated, aircraft manufacturers began to question whether a dedicated third crew member was still necessary. Boeing's subsequent 757 and 767 programs would answer that question.

The transition toward two-pilot commercial aircraft was already underway when Boeing began developing its 757 and 767 programs. Both aircraft entered service in the early 1980s, introducing advanced digital avionics and electronic flight displays that significantly reduced the need for conventional cockpit instrumentation. The 757 entered commercial service with Eastern Air Lines in January 1983, while the 767 followed later that year. Their integrated systems demonstrated that many functions previously requiring dedicated monitoring could be handled through computerized aircraft equipment. NASA's historical research into cockpit automation documents the technological changes introduced with the two aircraft, showing that the development was not entirely straightforward.

Boeing initially faced regulatory and industry resistance to operating larger aircraft with only two pilots. The 1981 Presidential Task Force on Aircraft Crew Complement examined whether advanced automation could safely absorb the responsibilities traditionally assigned to flight engineers. Its findings supported two-pilot operations and helped establish the regulatory foundation for aircraft such as the 767. NASA's publication, Human Factors of Advanced Technology Aircraft, explains how Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System (EICAS) technology became central to this transition. The system was even described as an electronic flight engineer because it could monitor aircraft systems and alert pilots when intervention was necessary.

Contrary to popular belief, the Boeing 747-400 was not the first four-engine jet aircraft certified for two-pilot operation. That distinction belongs to the Lockheed JetStar, the first quadjet designed for two-pilot operation, introduced into service in 1961. Meanwhile, the British Aerospace BAe 146, which first flew in 1981 and entered commercial service in 1983, is recognized as the first commercial passenger quadjet certified for a two-pilot flight deck. Before these developments, four-engine mainline jetliners traditionally required a flight engineer. Thus, the 747-400 did not invent the concept, but it extended that philosophy to the jumbo-jet market.

First quadjet overall with two-pilot operations

First commercial passenger quadjet certified for two-pilot operations

Established integrated systems monitoring

Extended two-pilot philosophy to the jumbo jet

Boeing already had the technological foundations in place when it decided to modernize its flagship aircraft. However, transferring the concept to the 747 required a much more extensive redesign than simply removing the flight engineer's seat.

As the last remaining commercial 747 aircraft near retirement, it still represents one of the most iconic eras in American aviation.

The Boeing 747-400 introduced a completely redesigned flight deck that replaced the traditional analog instrumentation with a computerized glass cockpit. Instead of presenting aircraft information through hundreds of individual gauges and switches, the new arrangement consolidated essential data into six cathode-ray tube (CRT) displays. Two primary flight displays and two navigation displays provided the pilots with essential flight information, while the central displays presented engine parameters and aircraft systems information. According to Airport Technology's technical overview of the 747-400, these displays measured about eight inches by eight inches and incorporated flight control, navigation, engine indication, and crew alerting information.

One of the most striking changes involved the number of instruments and controls in the cockpit. The integrated digital avionics systems reduced the number of flight deck lights, gauges, and switches from approximately 971 on the 747-300 to just 365 on the 747-400. This represented a reduction of more than 60%, illustrating how much information had been consolidated into electronic displays. The Aviamagazine Boeing 747 factsheet documents this transformation.

The aircraft's development also benefited from technology introduced on the 757 and 767. Boeing incorporated integrated avionics, computerized flight management, and more sophisticated monitoring systems, allowing information previously distributed across the flight engineer's panel to be presented directly to the pilots. The 747-400 entered commercial service with Northwest Airlines on February 9, 1989, marking a significant departure from the original jumbo jet's cockpit philosophy. Boeing-747.com's flight deck history explains how the redesigned cockpit absorbed the functions of the traditional engineering station.

As a result, the working environment for pilots changed substantially. However, the most important question was not how many instruments Boeing removed, but how the aircraft continued performing the responsibilities previously assigned to the third crew member.

Boeing did not transfer every flight engineer responsibility to the captain and first officer. Instead, it redesigned the aircraft's systems so that computers could continuously monitor many operating parameters and present the information requiring attention to the remaining crew members. One of the most important technologies was the Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System (EICAS), which consolidated engine information and aircraft system alerts into electronic displays. EICAS could identify abnormal conditions and communicate relevant information to both pilots, thus replacing a flight engineer who monitored hundreds of individual instruments.

The flight engineer's traditional responsibilities extended well beyond engine monitoring, and the new automated system had to cover them. The 747-400's integrated systems provided information about fuel distribution, electrical power, hydraulic systems, environmental controls, and other essential aircraft functions. Pilots could access additional system information through dedicated display pages, while alerts helped prioritize conditions requiring their attention. The Boeing 747-400 technical overview describes the integrated avionics architecture, including systems supplied by Rockwell Collins and Honeywell. In other words, the functions once spread across numerous instruments were consolidated into fewer electronic displays.

Nevertheless, automation did not eliminate the need for pilots to understand the aircraft's technical systems. The captain and first officer remained responsible for monitoring the aircraft, interpreting warnings, and deciding how to respond to abnormal situations. The computers could identify problems and provide information, but they could not replace the judgment required when making operational decisions. This distinction was important because the introduction of advanced avionics also created new human-factor challenges, including the possibility of pilots becoming overly dependent on automation. NASA's research into the introduction of new cockpit technology examined precisely these issues, including pilot workload, training, and the interaction between flight crews and computerized systems.

In short, the 747-400 redistributed responsibilities rather than eliminating an entire operational function. Integrated aircraft systems began performing the flight engineer's traditional monitoring tasks, while the remaining crew members supervised them. This also changed the economics of operating the jumbo jet, particularly on long-haul routes where crew scheduling and staffing represented significant recurring expenses.

Technological advancements in the cockpit enable modern aircraft to fly with only two pilots.

Many airlines had important commercial implications with the introduction of the two-pilot 747-400 configuration. Removing the dedicated flight engineer position meant operators no longer needed to roster a third specialist for every flight, reducing cockpit staffing requirements and simplifying crew scheduling. On long-haul operations, where extended duty periods could require additional pilots, this was particularly valuable. It also made the 747-400 more consistent with the two-pilot philosophy already established on the Boeing 757 and 767, helping airlines operating multiple Boeing aircraft families benefit from a more standardized approach to cockpit operations.

The 747-400's commercial success demonstrated the importance of this modernization. Boeing produced 694 examples of the variant, making it the most commercially successful passenger generation of the jumbo jet family. Its appeal was not based exclusively on the new cockpit, as the aircraft also introduced winglets, improved engines, greater range, and other aerodynamic and structural refinements. Nevertheless, the two-pilot flight deck was among its most consequential operational improvements. The aircraft's success helped establish the expectation that even large four-engine widebodies could operate without a dedicated flight engineer.

Boeing continued this philosophy with the 747-8, the latest production generation of the jumbo jet. Introduced in passenger and freighter configurations, the 747-8 retained the two-pilot flight deck while incorporating further advances in avionics and electronic displays. Its cockpit included technology derived from the Boeing 787 program, although Boeing maintained sufficient commonality with the 747-400 to support a shared type rating following appropriate differences training. The aircraft therefore continued the transition that had begun with the -400, rather than returning to the three-person flight deck of earlier generations.

The 747-8 ultimately demonstrated that the two-pilot arrangement was not a temporary solution specific to the 747-400. It had become the established operating philosophy for the entire modern jumbo-jet family. However, the broader question remains relevant as commercial aircraft become increasingly automated: how much responsibility should be delegated to computers, and how can manufacturers ensure that pilots remain fully capable of managing the aircraft when those systems encounter problems?

The Boeing 747-400 demonstrated that technological advances could fundamentally change how airlines operated their largest aircraft, replacing extensive manual monitoring with integrated computer systems and electronic displays. The transition also helped establish a new relationship between pilots and automation, with computers handling routine monitoring tasks while flight crews retained responsibility for aircraft control and operational decisions.

The contrast between the 747-300 and 747-400 remains particularly striking. The former required three flight deck crew members and analog cockpit lights, gauges, and switches, while the latter operated with two pilots and a glass cockpit. The subsequent 747-8 continued the two-pilot configuration, confirming that Boeing considered the arrangement integral to the jumbo jet's modern design philosophy.

Although the older Lockheed JetStar and BAe 146 had already shown that four-engine aircraft could operate with two pilots, the 747-400 took this concept to an entirely different level in commercial aviation. It proved that aircraft size and engine count did not automatically determine cockpit crew requirements. The 747’s greatest legacy was demonstrating that computerization could transform even the world's most recognizable jumbo jet.
